speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
External Affairs
peace in the Middle East; and also recognition of Arab nationalism based on Arab countries free of Soviet communist threats, free of penetration and subversion, each one governing itself as it desires without interference from or without interfering in neighbouring states.
The second objective is collective security for defence against aggression. That certainly has been an objective of the British government over recent years in this area. The west, led by the British government, has tried to promote that objective of collective security through the Baghdad pact, which, we must not forget, it was hoped would embrace all the Arab states but which has never succeeded in doing so. However, it has split the Arab world into two camps, with the United Kingdom and the United States in one camp or at least with the United States half way in that camp and the other forces in the other camp.
I suggest that the third end that is being sought is security for oil supplies in that area which are vitally important to the whole economy of western Europe and, to a lesser extent, to other parts of the world; the security of navigation through the Suez canal, and the maintenance of legitimate western economic and other interests in the area.
Finally, I suggest as an objective of western policy in that area the right of Israel to a national existence within recognized and agreed boundaries. Of course there have been other objectives and policies, but perhaps these are the main ones.
A couple of weeks ago the violent and sudden overthrow of a friendly regime in Iraq seemed to strike at those policies and to foreshadow not only the end of the Baghdad pact but the revolutionary absorption of Lebanon and Jordan into the United Arab Republic; hence the intervention.
Again the question arises, does the intervention which has taken place strengthen and safeguard the objectives I have mentioned or does it serve to prevent some of the undesirable results which I have also mentioned? I doubt the first, though I admit the pressure which appeared to necessitate intervention at the time. I also admit the possibility of unhappy consequences if the action had not been taken. Presumably there was not very much time. That is one of the tragedies of international affairs these present days; there is never enough time to assess the consequences of action or no action. Presumably on this occasion there was not enough time, certainly not very much time, in which to weigh the disadvantages or advantages of intervention or no intervention because-and this is one of the most worrying features of the whole situation so far as

I am concerned-the outbreak in Iraq seems to have caught the western countries which have the most in the way of intelligence services completely by surprise. Yet we are now told by the authors of this revolution that they had been plotting it for months and years.
It is also now clear, and the minister mentioned this this morning-at least I believe he mentioned it, though if I am misinterpreting what he said he will correct me -that the governments of the United Kingdom and the United States are anxious to liquidate their intervention as quickly as possible and replace their forces by those once again, of the United Nations, for the important purpose of establishing and maintaining the right of Lebanon and Jordan not to be gobbled up, if I can put it that way. That is an understandable policy on the part of London and Washington because it is difficult, at least it is difficult for me, to see anything but difficulty ahead if this intervention has to be maintained.
We ask ourselves this question. Will the United States intervention in Lebanon increase the interference and aid for the rebels from outside, to prevent which was one of the purposes of the intervention? We read in the newspapers today, that the foreign minister of Lebanon is again complaining of assistance to the rebels from outside which he says has increased during the last week.
Another question we can hardly refrain from asking ourselves is what is the continuing objective of the intervention? What happens if King Hussein goes, or if he moves out of Jordan against Iraq? And above all, what effect will this intervention have on Arab nationalism in Lebanon, Jordan and elsewhere? Mr. Hanson Baldwin, writing in the New York Times on July 16, had this to say:
Their mere presence-
That is the mere presence of the United States forces.

in Lebanon will be to Arab nationalists like a red rag to a bull-it will do more than any other event since the Port Said attack to knit together Arab nationalists throughout the Middle East and to inflame them . . . the forces of Arab nationalism, symbolized by President Gamal Abdel Nasser of Egypt, will ultimately be strengthened-not weakened-by the United States action.
The London Economist gave expression to the same thought in a recent edition, and then there is another question that these governments must now be asking themselves. What about the security of the oil pipe lines if popular passions against western intervention should boil over?

However, the most important question of all is what should we do about the situation generally. I was glad to hear the minister say this morning that it is now time to look ahead and perhaps, in attempting to answer the question "What should we do about it?", we are looking ahead. My own effort to answer the question is as follows. I suggest we should recognize that the present situation in the Middle East is very much to the liking of Mr. Khrushchev of the Soviet union, who must be very happy at this western intervention since its major result may well be to stir up anti-western feeling, and who benefits most by this feeling in any part of the world. In that sense perhaps this kind of action is really playing the Russian game. I suggest that Mr. Khrushchev, in spite of all his recent words, may not have any great desire to see the United States and the United Kingdom leave these countries. I believe, however, that he has a very great desire to secure the maximum propaganda out of their being there.
I submit that the second aspect, the second phase of the policy we should adopt, which follows from my answer to the first question, is the withdrawal as soon as possible from these countries by the United Kingdom and the United States, in accordance with the desire they have themselves expressed. However, as we all know it is much easier to land troops in an emergency than it is to withdraw them, and sometimes it is not easy to avoid getting enmeshed even further than was originally intended.
This is where the United Nations comes in, and I am glad to see that that organization is playing its part. The United Nations could help make possible the withdrawal of these forces, which is the desire of the two governments concerned, and perhaps this assistance can now be obtained. It is going to be difficult to negotiate in the security council, as my hon. friend knows, because of the veto used by the Russians with respect to action in that council. Assistance may be obtained, however, through a summit meeting, although a good deal of confusion seems to now be developing over the calling and the composition of such a meeting. It was only a few days ago that we discussed this matter in this house, when Mr. Khrushchev issued his invitation to discuss the Middle East question at a summit meeting.
It seems to me that this was a suggestion which the two powers most concerned, Great Britain and the United States, should have taken up at once, especially in so far as the terms put forward by Mr. Khrushchev regarding the composition were concerned, although they certainly could not have accepted the form of the invitation which was, to
External Affairs
say the least, offensive in character. Surely, however, they could have replied at once that the invitation was acceptable in the sense that the four powers and the secretary general should meet, and meet quickly, and that the meeting should be held under the auspices of the security council.
I personally felt at that time, and I still feel-even more so in the light of developments in the last day or two-that it would have been a good thing for the security council to have been called together at once. They could have set up a committee of the council to consist of the four countries plus India and the secretary general of the United Nations, as mentioned in the invitation of Mr. Khrushchev. Under the chairmanship of the secretary general that committee could have commenced work right away in any place recommended or chosen by the secretary general, with the agreement of the governments concerned. He may well have chosen, although of course I do not know this, Geneva; and while it is not possible for any summit conference to be held without a good deal of publicity, perhaps there might be a little less publicity in Geneva than on the east side of New York.
I do feel, even more strongly than I did a few days ago, that the represention put forward by Mr. Khrushchev for this meeting was a very advantageous one from the point of view of the west, because of its inclusion of the United Kingdom, the United States, France, India-a member of the commonwealth-and the secretary general. I suggest we are now getting away from that sort of clear-cut composition. The press reports would indicate that there is a good deal of manoeuvring going on, not only as to where the meeting should be held but also as to who should attend. Perhaps a solution will be found in a full meeting of the security council, with additional countries invited who have special interests in the problem, as Mr. Khrushchev has suggested, and after a first or second meeting at the summit in the security council in New York perhaps then the countries which were originally mentioned by Mr. Khrushchev might meet under the chairmanship of the secretary general in private sessions, as indeed was the practice during the Suez discussions at New York I think three years ago this summer.
But I cannot myself feel too optimistic about a full meeting of the security council to discuss Middle Eastern matters in this tense and excitable atmosphere with additional governments invited, as Mr. Khrushchev has suggested, to a number not yet determined; a meeting to be held in New York in public in the United Nations. I am

External Affairs
afraid it will be difficult to avoid that kind of public meeting becoming an instrument merely of propaganda.
Mr. Walter Lippmann, who is a pretty wise commentator on these matters, I think, had this to say this morning in his column in the Montreal Gazette:
As things stand at this moment, the notion of a summit meeting in the heart of New York city has the characteristic of one of those nightmares in which one feels compelled to do what one desperately does not want to do.
At this time, a public confrontation between Eisenhower and Khrushchev would be a ghastly spectacle, almost certain to poison the air still further with charges and counter-charges.
I do not think we have to be as pessimistic as that but I do hope, and I feel certain my hope is shared by the government, that if this meeting takes place in the full security council in New York, then advantage will be taken at the earliest opportunity of arranging small and confidential meetings of those most concerned to be held under the auspices of the secretary general himself.
There are two other questions to be considered with regard to policy in the Middle East. After withdrawal, the United Nations I think should move in, if the circumstances require it, and if authority can be secured from the security council, or if not from the United Nations assembly. In referring to moving in I do not want to be too dogmatic as to how it should be done. One way would be by a United Nations emergency force, but another would be the way pointed out by the minister this morning, by strengthening the existing United Nations observer group to a point where it might be able to exercise a pacifying and stabilizing influence in the country in which it is operating.
We on this side heard with much satisfaction the statement of the minister to the effect that the government is prepared to support to the fullest extent action to strengthen that group of United Nations observers. It is encouraging to read in the press that the secretary general, without requiring a further resolution from the security council, has already taken advantage of an earlier resolution to strengthen the observer group. This constitutes another debt we owe to a man of exceptional quality, integrity and ability, the secretary general of the United Nations.
What we have been going through during the last two or three weeks-and I mentioned this earlier in my statement, before lunch- has served to underline and emphasize the necessity of a permanent United Nations emergency force. I do not mean by that 20,000 or 25,000 soldiers in a camp of their

own in some country chosen for that purpose. I mean a force consisting of contingents earmarked and available for service at the request of the United Nations authorities; ready to serve at a moment's notice, forces earmarked by other than permanent members of the security council that would be kept available in their own country for such United Nations service.

pointed out, Mr. Speaker, it was attempted more than once. It was attempted under the provisions of the charter which provide for an international force under the security council. speechtext:
Under article 43 of the
charter, as my hon. friend mentions. I think that this permanent military staff is still in existence, nominally, and I am not sure that it does not even meet once a month or so. It consists of military officers from permanent members of the council. It was frustrated from the beginning by the failure of those members of the council to agree on anything, let alone building up force behind the charter. While it became clear over the years that it could not be done in that way, the Prime Minister will recall that during the Korean crisis the first steps were taken by which the assembly could move in to organize forces when the security council was paralysed by the veto. That was done by an assembly resolution which was called the "Uniting for Peace" resolution. That was the resolution used during the Suez crisis to build up on an ad hoc basis a force which I believe was of assistance and which I believe is still doing good service in that part of the world.
That was done under emergency conditions. The Prime Minister will remember that within 48 hours of the resolution of the United Nations assembly authorizing the creation of this force, the force was formally in existence, and within 72 hours the first members of the force were on the job. But surely we

should not rely on that kind of thing in an emergency. Surely it would be better using the assembly resolution for this purpose, if we cannot do it through the security council, to set up in the countries concerned -and they would have to be the non-permanent members of the security council, omitting the big powers-contingents which would be available for this kind of service if the assembly or the security council requested it; which would be organized for that purpose and which could move into action without delay.
I know that this has been attempted in the last year. I think it was brought up at the last assembly. X am not in a position to criticize anyone because it has not been done, for we have all been trying to do it. But perhaps this second demonstration in an international crisis of the value of this kind of police organism in permanent existence will give us now more chance of success in following the matter up at the next assembly than we had at previous assemblies. That is all I am putting forward at this time.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on that point would the hon. gentleman permit a question. The hon. gentleman used the expression "move into action". Did he mean into military action, or would he care to change that expression?

speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker; that was perhaps a careless expression. I meant that it could be moved into police and supervisory action. I know perhaps as well as most hon. members of the house the limitation of this kind of force and indeed the limitation of this kind of action. This force would be of no value at all as a military force in the normal sense. It could not stand up against a big or a middle power. If there were a dispute between the big powers this force would be futile. But as a police force operating as it did in Palestine, and operating as it might in the Middle East now under the authority of the United Nations for police purposes, it might be of great value. All I am suggesting is that if it has any possible value of that kind, that value would be very greatly increased by having the force ready to go into this kind of action when required.
But more important perhaps than the questions I have brought up as to the future policy toward this area is the necessity of following up this immediate crisis by some kind of economic and political solution for problems of the whole area, and I was delighted to hear the minister express that thought this morning. Withdrawal and perhaps replacement by a United Nations police force will not be enough unless we do some-
External Affairs
thing about the political and economic difficulties that brought about the situation in the first place.
I recall very well and with a tragic memory that while in the Suez crisis we may have succeeded in producing a United Nations police force which was of help in that crisis, we failed in our major objective, which was to take advantage of that atmosphere of crisis and do something about the political and economic difficulties between Israel and her neighbours which brought about the crisis in the first place. We did nothing on that front; therefore we did not succeed there even though we may have succeeded in the more limited field of preventing the conflict spreading.
We hope we will not make that mistake this time. I know how easy it will be to make such a mistake after the immediate crisis is solved, but I hope that this time the west will try to work out on a firm and permanent basis its relations with those nationalist forces in that area I have been talking about. I believe that for this purpose the west-and I am thinking of the United States, the United Kingdom and France particularly-must base their relations with those countries on the acceptance of Arab nationalism and of the United Arab Republic; must try to bring about as much co-operation as possible with those forces; try to remove the suspicions which have been engendered over the past and which are not by any means all the fault of the west. They must accept the realities of the present and base their policy on the fact that the nineteenth century is dead and is not likely to return.
I suggest something else, and this is going to be even more difficult politically; that our policy in the Middle East in the future must recognize that the U.S.S.R. has both interest and power in that area. Indeed its power in that area is far greater than that which could be produced in the west to bear upon the problems of that area at any given time. I think we must all be very conscious of the fact that while there are 10,000 United States marines in Lebanon and two or three British paratroop battalions in Jordan, there are 23 Soviet divisions, it is reported, strung along the Iran-Turkish border. Therefore it is idle to pretend the Soviet union need only be tolerating that area. It is also idle to deny the fact that the Soviet union has very real interests in that area which perhaps should be recognized.
The minister said this morning that one of the happy developments of recent years, and a development which might be applied to the Middle East, was the successful operation of the international commissions in Indo-China.

External Affairs
I agree with him, though I also agree with him when he said the time has come to wind up the activities of two of those commissions in the way he mentioned. But he himself also said-and it is an important fact-that in that operation in Indo-China one of the three members of each commission was from a communist state. While it is true that it is a state which is making moves toward communist nationalism, yet at the time it was appointed it was pretty close to the foreign policy and the defence policy of Russia. That was recognized at that time and I was at the Geneva conference when it was accepted that there could be no settlement of the kind desired in Indo-China without a recognition of the participation of the communist world in that settlement. It was done, and the results have not been too bad.
Perhaps if we are going to have a final economic and political settlement in the Middle East we will have to recognize in some appropriate way the interest of the Soviet in that settlement. Perhaps the best way to do that would be to bring any political and economic aid scheme-the minister mentioned it this morning-into the United Nations; a Marshall plan, if you want to call it that, for the Middle East but administered by the United Nations, where perhaps Soviet participation will be less open to exploitation than if it were done in any other way. Indeed they may not wish to participate at all in that kind of plan.
Then finally Mr. Speaker-it will be an important phase of our policy in this area in the future-that we have to continue in the west to give support to Israel's right to a secure national existence. We have got to do more than that with Israel's co-operation and assistance. We have to think of some way of liquidating the Arab refugee problem.
This is a very sketchy outline of the basis of our policy in the Middle East, a policy which I think provides the best hope of strengthening legitimate western influence and strength in that area and at the same time strengthening the chances of peace and security.
The alternative is the pursuit of power politics without sufficient power, or at least sufficient power in the face of the hostility of another and nearer great power which can bring more power to bear on that particular area. That is one alternative, and I certainly hope we will not follow it. But an even worse alternative than that, perhaps, is a policy of drift and uncertainty; of trying to pursue contradictory aims and trying to execute those contradictory aims in a halfhearted and confused way. I suggest the policy which I have ventured to outline in
[Mr. Pearson.l
brief is one of realism and common sense, and one which the west should pursue at this time.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I had hoped to deal with a good many other subjects, but I do not want to take up all the time of the house on this debate. I probably will have another opportunity to discuss these matters. I was going to talk about NATO and its importance in many things, and particularly in this Middle East crisis. I was glad to read in the press this morning that the NATO council is meeting today, as it has been meeting in recent days, to consider developments in the Middle East. It is of the greatest possible importance to strengthen political cooperation through the NATO council not only in the area covered by NATO but in the areas contiguous to the NATO countries which are of vital importance to them.
I also suggest that political co-operation in NATO requires a solution of the difficulties between its members with special interest in the Middle East. Something must be done, for instance to halt the growing bitterness and enmity between the two NATO countries, Turkey and Greece. I have stated a good many times, my view that a military and defence foundation for NATO is not enough, indeed it is necessary now as it was never necessary before to make progress in the field of economic and political co-operation.
Then, Mr. Speaker, there is the most important question of all, and this concerns not merely the Middle East, which is a reflection of the importance of this general question. What can we do at this time to ease tensions and remove or diminish some of the dangers of war? The minister touched upon the matter this morning, but it really deserves far more time than we can give to it in a debate of this kind. But I suggest, however, as I have suggested many times, that we should not allow the crises of the moment to prevent us continuing to seek solutions of our problems with the Soviet union through diplomatic and political channels. We should not only keep our defence strong-we have to do that, though it is a little difficult these days to know what kind of defence should be kept-but we have to keep our diplomacy enlightened and imaginative and vigorous.
The fact that we all feel-and I think we have felt it more in the last two weeks than for quite a long time-the fear of what we call in diplomacy brinkmanship should not obscure the fact that even without that kind of diplomacy, even without those tactics which at times may worry us, even without brinkmanship, we remain on the brink of

extinction. This is true because of the developments in nuclear warfare, because of the piling up of weapons of mass destruction which if they are ever used can make life on this planet impossible. We do not need brinkmanship to emphasize that we are indeed on the brink of that kind of extinction if we allow diplomacy to degenerate into conflict or the world to slide into general war, which is perhaps the only way we will get in. We have existed in this way now for more than 10 years.
We have existed in a world which is bedevilled by a combination, as I have put it before, of hate and hydrogen, of fear and ferocity. That combination still overhangs our life. Our policy surely in this country, and in all free countries, must be to bring about the replacement of that kind of thing by some form of security, on the basis at least of mutual toleration, if we cannot do any better than that, between those who must coexist but cannot co-operate, plus-and this is equally important-closer and closer co-operation between those states which can and must work together for their very survival. That, I suggest to the house, is the only policy that makes sense today. We are all proud as Canadians to know that Canada has played, and I am sure is playing and will continue to play, a good and proud part in the pursuit of that policy. Perhaps I know as well as most Canadians how terribly difficult this part is, how exhausting at times it is and, as I said at the beginning of my statement and as the minister must have found, -how frustrating it often is. At times it seems so much easier to fall back into our foxholes, into our national trenches, to dig ourselves in there and wait for what may happen. Movement is hard and at times we wonder where we are going; or if we are going anywhere. We reach a green pasture and we find that there is a greener pasture beyond. We scale a peak and we find a higher one barring the way. As a poet puts it, "We are forever climbing the ever-mounting slope". But I know all members of the house will agree with me when I say that is no reason for giving up but is a reason for continuing to climb.
I know the house will also agree with me when I say that in this search for peace in a better world all members of the house, irrespective of the party to which they may belong, as indeed all Canadians, will be happy and proud to work together.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is without doubt an important day in the present session. An opportunity is accorded for the free expression of the views of members with respect to international
External Affairs
affairs and the crises that face our country and all countries of the world. It is to me, of course, a very unexpected and unusual experience to have to follow the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Smith) of the present government and the secretary of state for external affairs of the previous government. I am the first one to admit, sir, that I do not know the intricacies and strategies of inner diplomacy as they must be known by the two previous speakers because of the present position of the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the past experience of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson).
Therefore it follows that I do not intend to go into the intricate details of strategy or policy, but I do welcome this opportunity to put forward a few general thoughts from the viewpoint of a layman. I feel quite certain that in taking part in the first discussion of external affairs this session we can all start from the same fundamental belief, namely that nobody wants to see another world war. On that premise we have to consider developments as they occur.
In the present century the major countries of the world have seen two world wars in which countless billions of dollars in productive effort have been expended in the holocaust of war. In addition millions of men, women and children have either died or been mutilated. No one wants to see that happen again, and in saying that we have particular reference to the scientific and technological developments of recent years from which it is known by all that a third world war could possibly mean the annihilation of civilization as we understand it at the present time.
This leads me to make the observation that a world war can start from a spark in international relations in the same way as a catastrophic fire. In my own province of British Columbia right now there are almost one million acres on fire, a fire that could have started from a bolt of lightning, a carelessly thrown match or a cigarette that was not put out. So it is in war. Officially at least the first world war started because an archduke was assassinated. Officially at least the second world war started because of the aggression of one country, because of the insanity of one man.
That leads us, therefore, to the realization that as nobody wants to see another world war, very close attention must be paid to international affairs and relationships to see that with modern weapons, technology and science no spark occurs to lead the world into a conflagration which could mean the end of civilization. If that is accepted, and I think logically it may well be, we have to approach our external affairs and relationships not only on the basis of day to day

External Affairs
developments but on the basis of what has given rise to these developments.
There may be those who will not agree with me, which is understandable, but I quite honestly feel that if we are truly going to play our part and take every possible action to preserve peace we must understand what gives rise to certain actions by certain countries. In the past few years our major troubles have developed in the Middle East.
I have not yet seen any factual denial that even in connection with the Suez crisis it was not a matter of country against country but was a matter of the protection of oil interests. In these past few weeks we have again seen a Middle East crisis. I believe it would mean a great deal if we could be told whether or not the armed intervention was on an anti-communist basis or for the protection of certain oil interests. Personally, I am not going to state any conclusion, but I do consider this something upon which there has not been any government consideration or public answer.
I am convinced that nobody wants war. We can make the definite statement that Canada does not want war, nor do I believe that any of the western democracies want war. In view of that fact, I am led to ask if Canada could not play a greater part in advising on the present international crisis? We recognize that Canada is not a major power in the world but it is, if I can use the terms, a middle power. It is my definite belief that because Canada at no time has had imperialistic or colonial ambitions, and because of its economic strength Canada could play a most significant role in these very critical days.
When this present Middle East crisis developed I will say I was most disappointed in the first pronouncements that were made by this government. I interpreted them, and I think the majority of the press across Canada interpreted the statements as unqualified support of United States policy. I hasten to add that it was with appreciation and gratitude that, in very short order, we did see leadership and direction coming from the government, and not a supine following of the United States. There was a recognition of the seriousness of the situation, and very definite representations to deal with the crisis. Personally, I feel proud of the direction that was given after the first pronouncement, and I hope that direction may have had some effect upon the developments of recent days and the changed policies. The result has been that Canada has given some leadership on the calling of a summit meeting.
I listened very intently to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Smith) in

what he had to say today, but I have one regret. He failed to give to this house any indication of how strong a position Canada is going to take in view of the recent pronouncements made by, or on behalf of, the President of the United States. We in this corner of the house believed even up until yesterday that some country of the western world had to speak very clearly and bluntly to the United States about its foreign policy with regard to the present Middle East situation. Personally, I cannot understand why, if we truly believe that our economy is the best in the world, that our democracy is the best, we are afraid-when I say "we" I mean as western democratic powers-to meet with anybody else in this world face to face. Quite honestly, Mr. Speaker, I think that the prestige, the influence of the free powers has slipped within the past few days if what appears in the press is correct. According to press reports the government of the United States is disturbed that Khrushchev has accepted the invitation to a summit meeting in New York. There are statements, and perhaps we will have more information about them, that they fear Khrushchev would use such a meeting for propaganda purposes.
I am not going to go into any more detail about that, Mr. Speaker, except to say that if we believe in our way of life, if we believe in our democratic system, then we need have no fear of meeting the leader of any country, any time, anywhere, especially if it may be the basis upon which some agreement may be reached to settle the present mid-eastem crisis and prevent a conflict that could possibly lead to a third world war.
This is a general discussion on external affairs, so may I add this. I know it is of importance to the Prime Minister (Mr. Dief-enbaker) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs, but I direct my remarks in particular to the Prime Minister: I am not in any way derogatory of efforts made by his government or the previous government towards the cessation of nuclear tests or on behalf of world disarmament. But I should like, on behalf of the group in this corner of the house, to ask if still greater emphasis could not De put upon the efforts of the Prime Minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs as between their counterparts in other governments, in the United Nations security council, the United Nations general assembly and special committees, to drive home the absolute essentiality of the cessation of nuclear tests for war purposes and disarmament if we are to avoid another world war.
We must be honest at all times. Today we have a world armament race; you can call it a defence against another country but the

other country is saying the same thing. So whilst we work on defence, we also work on offence. I think the history of the world proves that if you build weapons of offence and defence, eventually you use them. As I said before, I am saying nothing derogatory on what the Prime Minister has worked for in the past. I am just asking that in following up-and I am certain the direction has come from the Prime Minister in the present Middle East crisis-that additional emphasis be placed along the lines which I have just suggested.
We in this group completely agree-and we emphasize this point-that you cannot sit on the fence or play both ends against the middle. The western powers agree on collective security or they do not. We believe in collective security. If we are going to have collective security in the democratic countries it must not be broken down or betrayed. That is why in this house and in our convention which is still going on in Montreal we have expressed our regrets and our condemnation of the countries-yes, of the United States to the south of us and the United Kingdom in which I was born-taking independent action in the landing of troops of their own volition without going through the collective security agency which we are trying to build up, which we support and in which we are all partners. If the United Nations general assembly means anything or if the United Nations security council means anything and if it is going to have a proper respect in this world, it must be because those who are partners in it follow through on collective action. Anything else is not only a betrayal of the meaning of collective security but is making a gift of a propaganda weapon and putting it in the hands of those who we are told are our enemies and who will use it to best advantage.
Mr. Speaker, I said just a few words this afternoon about the exigencies of absence. Very often the Prime Minister, because of the responsibilities of his office, is obliged to be away. We all understand that. Various cabinet ministers, because of their responsibilities and the exigencies of their offices, also are obliged to be away. Private members also very often are obliged to be away. We in our group find ourselves in a similar position because our biennial convention is being held this week and, as I think you will all understand, it is rather important that some M.P.'s be at that convention to discuss national and international politics. Unfortunately, I was not able to be there. However, learning that certain members were not able to return in time for this discussion this afternoon, I was on the telephone for about 30 minutes speaking to a colleague in Montreal in between the
External Affairs
lunch hour and now. We are a democratic party and hold a democratic convention representative of our movement across the length and breadth of Canada. I said, "I am going to have to speak this afternoon. What is the viewpoint of the national convention representative of our movement all across Canada with regard to the present situation?"

I have been talking here completely extemporaneously. I have not a solitary note. But knowing the kind of thinking that some people do, having expressed myself completely without a solitary note I thought I should give you the decision of our democratic movement; and that will show you up, my friend. This resolution was passed by our movement:
The present crisis in the Middle East is a direct result of the failure of the western powers to evolve a constructive policy based on the legitimate aspirations of the Arab peoples for freedom from outside domination and for social and economic advances and the legitimate aspirations of the people of Israel for a durable and viable peace with their Arab neighbours.
It is also the result of the deliberate subversion of these aspirations by ambitious men and forces both within and without the Middle East.
The C.C.F. has always opposed militarism and totalitarianism in all their forms. It has always censured military intervention whether it be in Hungary, Poland, Suez, Lebanon, Jordan or elsewhere.
It has always urged and urges today that international police action should be undertaken only through the United Nations if peace is to be achieved.
This convention of the C.C.F. therefore condemns the military intervention of the American and British governments in Lebanon and Jordan.
It also censures our own Canadian government which, in the initial stages at least, condoned and supported an action which was clearly an irresponsible risk of nuclear war.
However, the very urgency of the crisis gives the nations of the world an opportunity to lay the foundations of a permanent peace in the area along the following lines:
1.	The American and British forces should be withdrawn immediately, and replaced, if necessary, by a United Nations force composed of nationals of other than the major powers.
2.	In the meantime, all the great powers, as well as the neighbouring states stay out of Iraq.
3.	An immediate meeting at the summit should be held preferably through the United Nations to work out solutions not only for the present crisis, but for the economic and political problems in the area which present a constant threat to the peace of the world.

External Affairs
4.	A guarantee by the United Nations, to which the great powers are collectively committed, of all the nations in the area, including the state of Israel, against aggressive action.
5.	In order that conditions permitting lasting peace in the Middle East can be established, oil resources should be transferred in a peaceful and orderly fashion to the ownership and control of the Arab peoples and to this end the United Nations should offer to establish an international Middle East development commission, to assist the economic development of the area and ensure the raising of living standards for the people of these areas. Only such a broad and constructive approach to the problems of the area can end the legacy of hatred and dangers that threatens to engulf the whole world.
This convention therefore demands-
They say demand but I say request, sir.
-that the government of Canada pursue these policies unequivocally and vigorously at the United Nations and seek to unite all middle and small powers in a determined effort to achieve a peaceful and constructive settlement of the perilous situation in the Middle East.
I had a very good reason, Mr. Speaker, for wanting to place on the record at this time a decision made only within recent hours at the national convention of the C.C.F. This was because on the occasion of another debate in this house, when we were discussing national and international affairs, some hon. members, including the Prime Minister-as a matter of fact it was the Prime Minister who raised the issue and said that I and other members were saying something different to what had been passed at a provincial convention. This was when we were discussing NORAD and the Prime Minister read a news report with a good deal of relish. I do not blame him, for it was good politics. But I am a federal member, we are all federal members, in this house, and in the Prime Minister's party and in that of the Liberals and also among ourselves there are differences of opinion in localities and provinces, but national and international policy is laid down in the C.C.F. by a national convention. This is the national convention policy on the issue which we now face and I give it to the house unequivocally.
I am now about to draw my remarks to a dose. I am sure the Prime Minister knows the importance of this matter but I wish to commend to his attention the fact-and this I wish to emphasize-that Canada can exercise great influence and leadership but that the guidance must come from the Prime Minister himself through, of course, his ministers. I think upon consideration he will agree that emphasis would not be misplaced on the banning of nuclear tests and the working towards disarmament in this crisis or in any future one. That action should not be taken by individual countries but only under the United Nations as a collective action when it is found to be necessary in the

interest of the maintenance of peace. Forces should not, moreover, be landed in any country in the uniform of any particular nation but only under the aegis of the United Nations emergency force.
The Prime Minister and I, belonging as we do to different parties, perhaps have a different outlook on fundamental philosophy, politically speaking, but we have had two world wars in our time and nobody wants another. It is unfortunate that power politics are being played by two great nations but it is my belief that this country, small as it may be, might nevertheless be able by its sense of direction and sanity to maintain peace throughout the world. I am but one of a group of eight members in this house, but this is my thinking which I commend to the Prime Minister for his consideration.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take advantage of this debate on external affairs to report to the house on Canada's participation in a very important international gathering which took place some three or four months ago. It will not of course be on the lofty level on which this debate has so far been conducted but it will be a proud story nevertheless.
I am going to digress if I may-I feel in one way that I should not, but I cannot help but pass this observation. I am sure the house listened with interest to the statement of policy of the C.C.F., particularly because many of us recall the varieties of C.C.F. policies on international affairs over the years. Back in the thirties, particularly around 1935 to 1937, the policy of the C.C.F. was, I believe, pacifism; by 1940, after our troops had gone abroad, the policy was to withdraw them from Europe and to sell our goods to both sides and to let the imperialistic powers fight it out; but 1945 the slogan was "Vote for the C.C.F. and help win the war". The varieties and shifts in C.C.F. policy will make one of the most interesting studies in Canada's history when the time comes some day to write the story of the rise and fall of this party.
My story today, however, deals with the international conference on the law of the sea held at the European headquarters of the United Nations in Geneva between February 24 and April 28 of this year. Sometimes in our preoccupation with the high principles and great hopes of the peoples of the world for the achievement of a family of nations living at peace with one another we forget the ordinary workaday procedures of the many hundreds of delegates and representatives of various countries who work, without the bright lights of publicity upon their

efforts, and yet move steadily forward in man's progress towards a more peaceful state. This report is a record of one of the more prosaic but none the less tangible steps forward made by mankind in its long and slow progress towards a peaceful civilization.
This conference is one of the most significant of international conferences of recent years and one that has achieved far-reaching results. It is true that much more was heard of the failure of the conference to reach agreement on the matter of fishing limits and the breadth of the territorial seas but may I remind the house and the nation that this was merely one article of 73. One hardly ever hears of the articles passed and which became part of international law, but this conference dealt with problems which were very complex and which had a tremendous range of conflicting interests, namely those of 86 different nations. In order to achieve any sort of agreement with so much complexity and among so many nations is in itself a very substantial achievement.
It will, I know, be a source of satisfaction to hon. members on all sides of the house to learn that during the deliberations the Canadian delegation played a leading role and its contribution, throughout the nine weeks of the conference, will long be remembered as one of the outstanding features of the conference. A good deal of the credit for this must go to the Honourable George Drew who gave such vigorous and imaginative leadership to the Canadian delegation and to the able and devoted team of officials who assisted Mr. Drew as members of that delegation. During my own brief visit to Geneva I was able to observe at first hand that Mr. Drew was regarded on all sides as one of the persons playing a very major part in the conference and one to whom the success of many of the negotiations was due.
It is worth while recalling here that the last conference of a similar type on the law of the sea was held at The Hague in 1930. It was known as The Hague codification conference. At that time some 40 nations participated and the international conference broke down on a single issue, the question of the breadth of the territorial sea. Twenty-eight years later with twice as many nations participating it seems rather significant that this same obstacle to agreement did not bring the conference to failure. The significant thing is that the participants achieved many things that went far beyond anything achieved in the whole history of international law since mankind first began to keep its history.
Specifically, the conference produced four international conventions as well as a protocol providing for the judicial settlement
External Affairs
of disputes. These four conventions were (1) a convention on the high seas; (2) a convention on fishing and the conservation of the living resources of the high seas; (3) a convention on the continental shelf; and (4) a convention on the territorial sea and contiguous zone. It was on April 29 that Mr. Drew signed these conventions on behalf of Canada as well as the protocol on the settlement of disputes and the final act of the conference. I might say that Canada was the first nation to sign all six of the instruments embodying the results of the conference. The four conventions and the protocol on the settlement of disputes are, of course, subject to ratification by the government of Canada and will not enter into force until ratified by at least 22 nations. Copies of these conventions have already been tabled by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Smith) and are reported in Votes and Proceedings of July 15.
Before dealing in more detail with the conventions and their significance to Canada it might be of interest to provide a little background on the events leading up to the conference and the method of work adopted by the conference. The conference was called as a result of a resolution by the general assembly of the United Nations on February 21, 1957-Resolution 1105X1. It grew out of the studies and recommendations made over the years by the international law commission of the United Nations which had been meeting since the initial formation of the United Nations in 1946. The commission had given very intensive study to all aspects of maritime law and then produced an extremely comprehensive report. It provided for 73 articles and was a compilation of all the rules of the sea which have been adopted over the years by the various nations. These 73 recommendations or rules have two different aspects to them. On the one hand they sought to codify all existing international law where there was already in existence extensive practice, precedent and doctrine. Then, on the other hand, they were concerned with the progressive development of international law on matters such as the continental shelf that were as yet largely unregulated because 30 years ago at The Hague conference they hardly thought of such a thing. And then, in addition, the conference was asked by the general assembly to consider a matter not included within the compass of the international law commission report the question of access to the sea by landlocked countries.
After a brief plenary session the conference resolved itself into five committees of the whole, each of which was charged with the

External Affairs
consideration of a group of related articles. The results of the committees' work were considered in the final plenary sessions during the last week of the conference. The committees and the subject matter referred to each were as follows: committee I, the territorial sea and contiguous zone, and specifically articles 1 to 25 and article 66 of the original I.L.C. report; committee II, the high seas, general regime, and specifically articles 26 to 48 and 61 to 65; committee III, the high seas, fishing, and specifically articles 48 to 60; committee IV, the continental shelf, and specifically articles 67 to 73; and committee V, access to the sea of landlocked countries. That was a new subject to be discussed at the conference itself. It will be seen that the breakdown of the conference into these five committees follows in general the subjects of the conventions I have already listed.
It may be of interest at this point to comment briefly on some of the results of the conference which were of particular significance to Canada. In commenting on this I might point out that for the first time in history there is now an international agreement on the continental shelf. I mention this first because it is usually lost sight of because this subject was uneventful in terms of news coverage and as far as producing quarrels or differences is concerned.
The continental shelf convention gives to the coastal state sovereign rights over the exploration and exploitation of the natural resources of the sea bed and subsoil off its coast out to a depth of 200 meters. It also provides that these rights may be exercised beyond that depth if the exploitation of the resources is a practical possibility. In the long term, this agreement may have consequences of far-reaching importance to Canada in the development of underwater oil and mineral resources. It means, in effect, a very substantial addition to the potential area of Canada's natural resources. Those who have followed with interest the development of techniques in the exploration of resources know that we can drill for oil at depths of 1,500 feet under the surface of the sea.
It is not without significance that it was a proposal put forward by Canada in committee IV that led to the adoption of the convention on the continental shelf nor is it without significance that it was a Canadian proposal to the final plenary session that led to a prohibition against reservations to the three main substantive articles in the convention. To have permitted these reservations might have undermined the whole purpose of the convention. Finally, it was not without significance that it was Canada which

proposed that this convention should enter into force when signed by 22 nations instead of 50 as proposed by another power.
The second convention dealt with fishing and the conservation of the living resources of the high seas. The convention on high seas fishing is the first such general convention regulating high seas fishing and it accords well with Canadian interests. It recognizes the special interest of the coastal state in maintaining the productivity of the living resources of the high seas in areas adjacent to its territorial sea. It also entitles the coastal state to take part on an equal footing in any system of research or regulation for purposes of conservation in that area even though its own nationals may not carry on fishing there. To all people who understand the importance of fishing to underdeveloped countries, the significance of this particular article is self-evident. Further, it provides that when conservation measures in the high seas have been adopted by a coastal state, they must be observed by fishermen from other countries. And then finally, under emergency circumstances, coastal states may unilaterally enact the necessary conservation measures on the high seas.
The third important feature to Canada was the question of straight base lines and bays. To those of us who live in the island portions of Canada the fact that our coastline is very irregular hardly comes to our attention but in trying to define territorial waters the sinuosity of our coastline is a matter that gives us considerable concern and therefore these regulations in this regard, as drafted and codified by this international law of the sea, are very important to the future of our country.
In the convention on the territorial sea and the contiguous zone, article 4 provides that where the coast is deeply indented the method of drawing straight base lines from headland to headland may be followed in setting the boundary of the territorial sea rather than following the sinuosities of the coastline. I think the importance of that can be realized. Thirdly, our shoreline now in so far as the territorial sea is concerned is not the line of the high water mark or the low water mark; it is a line drawn from headland to headland. This provision, which reflects the 1951 decision in the well-known Anglo-Norwegian fisheries case is of particular interest to Canada because much of our coastline is deeply indented, as I have already pointed out.
In the committee stage there was a move to impose a limitation of 15 miles on straight baselines which would have had undesirable

results for us. However, action by Canada in the plenary session was successful in having this limitation removed. The conference also adopted a provision recognizing that bays with mouths of 24 miles or less are to be regarded as internal waters. This limitation would not, of course, affect bays along coasts where the baseline system is applicable.
The fourth convention deals with the general law of the high seas. The convention on the high seas has perhaps less significance for Canada than the others because, in the main, it simply codifies existing international law. It provides for the first time a systematic compilation of recognized international law on a number of important matters and seeks to ensure the maximum freedom of the high seas. This applies not only to navigation but to fishing on the high seas, flying over the high seas and such activities as the laying of submarine cables and the building of pipe lines under the high seas.
Among other things, the convention deals with such matters as the nationality of ships, safety of life at sea, the suppression of piracy and the slave trade, the right of hot pursuit in certain circumstances and the prevention of pollution of the seas by the discharge of oil or the dumping of radioactive waste. It was, Mr. Speaker, a very thorough compilation of the existing laws of the sea into a code which we now hope will be ratified by the great majority of the nations of the world.
I have referred in brief summary, Mr. Speaker, to some of the highlights of the four conventions. Now I would like to turn to the question of the breadth of the territorial sea and the related question of coastal fishing zones. It is on this subject, of course, that the publicity was given which attracted such widespread public interest. It is unfortunate in one way that this aspect of the conference's work reached so much public interest because it tended to obscure many of the more constructive achievements of the conference. I would like to give some of the background of this matter of the breadth of the territorial sea to see whether we cannot make clear what the problem is and the importance of Canada's contribution so far and what we think it can be in the future.
There has been no uniform practice, Mr. Speaker, in so far as the breadth of the territorial sea is concerned. Generally speaking, the great maritime nations have accepted and enforced the three-mile territorial sea off the coasts of the various countries of the world. Many countries for many years have had breadths of the territorial sea off their countries of more than three miles. There are 57071-3-169
External Affairs
countries with a four-mile territorial sea; there are several with a six-mile territorial sea and there is one with a nine-mile territorial sea-that is Mexico-and the Soviet union has a 12-mile territorial sea. Some go beyond that, even to the extent of 200 miles. This great variety of claims on the breadth of the territorial sea indicates that there is no such thing as uniformity. Generally speaking, the maritime powers have insisted on and recognized only three miles, even though there has not been any direct challenge to the countries that have territorial seas of different widths. As a matter of interest, the U.S.S.R. has a territorial sea of 12 miles, going back to the days of the Czars and it is not likely that anyone is going to challenge anything that has been in existence for over 50 years.
Having given this background, I think it is now fitting for me to point out that this problem was so complex that the international law commission did not make any definite recommendations to this general conference of the United Nations on this matter, but simply pointed out that 12 miles in its opinion was the maximum limit that they thought should exist. Now, for some time Canada has felt that a 12-mile limit was necessary to protect our fishing interests but we have recognized that an extension of the territorial sea to 12 miles might jeopardize the proper interests of those nations and those people who want to maintain freedom of the sea and freedom for air navigation. Therefore, our dilemma was, how could we reconcile the defence interests, freedom of the seas and the freedom of the air, which really requires a very narrow territorial sea, and the needs of our people on our coasts for some priority in harvesting the fish off their shores?
It is a matter of general knowledge, Mr. Speaker, that at the present time by Canadian law we have forbidden Canadian trawlers to fish within 12 miles of our coasts, and yet, because there is no international law, the trawlers from foreign nations can come inside our 12-mile limit and do fish in waters that the Canadian people do not allow Canadian trawlers to fish in. Quite frankly, we would like to reserve those first 12 miles off our shores for the people who cannot afford the big trawlers and who would like to make a living out of this band of water that they can get to and from with their limited resources as far as capital equipment is concerned.
Now, that was the problem that we faced at this conference, and this goes back for several months and years. The Canadian government proposed what became known as the Canadian proposal. This was first put

I have just about concluded. I was pointing out that in this very important part of Canada's external relations, a part that does not show on the surface, delegations do go to conferences and achieve worth-while results. I have been asked two very important questions by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson). The first question was, what was the stand of the U.S.S.R.? At the conference the U.S.S.R. had a proposal that the width of the territorial sea should be 12 miles. Then they had an additional clause, over which the lawyers argued back and forth, which would seem to indicate that they believed the territorial sea should be 12 miles or more in certain cases. Their stand, informally, was that they would give support to the Canadian proposal, but that declaration was never made formally on the conference floor. However, countries like India and Mexico, had the definite impression that the U.S.S.R. and their satellite countries were very much in favour of guaranteeing to coastal states exclusive fishing rights for 12 miles.
Canada co-sponsored a proposal with Mexico and India, which more or less accepted the status quo by limiting the territorial sea to what nations already had in effect, and gave exclusive fishing rights up to 12 miles. When the Indians and Mexicans found out the Russians among others were not going to support this, they withdrew and our coalition fell apart. We went back to our original proposal. I might say that the attitude of the smaller nations, if I can report this accurately and I think I can, was one of intense disappointment that the U.S.S.R. position had been one thing in discussion but when the votes were down, and when it seemed possible Canada would get a two-thirds majority, they backed away from supporting us. This affected the good feeling that had existed between the U.S.S.R. and the Afro-Asian nations.
The second question deals with Iceland. We opposed at the conference the idea of any change any nation might make unilaterally, in the hope that there would be no unilateral declarations before a second conference. Since that time Iceland has declared that on September 1 she will have a 12-mile exclusive fishing zone off her territory. As you know, this has been opposed by the United Kingdom. Our stand is still the same. We do not think the answer lies in any nation unilaterally trying to establish any changes in the breadth of the territorial sea or establishing fishing rights in a larger zone, so long as there is any hope of achieving agreement through the United Nations.

Naturally enough, we would oppose such a matter being dealt with in any smaller regional groups because the subject affects nations all over the world. We have an obligation to our allies in this struggle to give to coastal nations some share of fishing off their coasts. We hope that these two civilized nations, Iceland and the United Kingdom, meeting together in some form of bilateral understanding, can resolve these differences or postpone them until they can be dealt with by the United Nations conference, which I hope will come next year.
I should like to repeat that I am quite confident, once we can get rid of the impact of these power blocs and the issue can be clearly dealt with on an economic basis that a decision can be arrived at supported by two-thirds of the nations of the world. If we can achieve some modus vivendi among traditional fishing countries in this period of adjustment, civilized nations dealing with this on a purely economic basis could resolve these differences. If we can achieve agreement on this article dealing with the breadth of the territorial sea and the breadth of the fishing zone off the coasts of our country, we will have achieved something that mankind has looked forward to for nearly 2,000 years.
I should like to close with a statement of my own as far as the visit to Geneva is concerned. I think I can report to the house, as can every other Canadian delegate who has been to any of these international conferences, the growing respect for Canada by people all over the world for our moderation and for the principles on which we operate. I think that we can play a great part which the United Kingdom and the United States cannot play.
Whether we like it or whether we do not, these newer nations of Africa and Asia- and to some extent this is true of the South American republics-sometimes are reluctant to rely too implicitly on the United States and the United Kingdom. To them they sometimes represent a form of something which they have been trying to get away from. At the same time these same nations in Africa and Asia do not want to come under the subjection of imperialistic power which does not give them any freedom whatsoever. They are looking for leadership of a moderate sort. In their minds Canada has no axe to grind. They feel that when we put forward a proposal that we are going to stick to the three-mile zone for the territorial sea and when we tell them why we want to support it, they tend to trust us; and when we advocate moderation on this question of the 12-mile limit they tend to follow us.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate, I realize of course the responsibility if not the risk I am taking, and the house will not expect me to venture into the intricacies of the diplomatic process. I do not intend to more than bring out a few general ideas which guide, as they must, our foreign policy.
In the light of developments in these last two weeks, it is appropriate, I believe, that our Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Smith) be warmly congratulated for the excellent job he has done in the interest of Canada and peace at United Nations. In my opinion, he has ably expressed Canada's position and like his predecessors, he was a credit to Canada.
The position taken by Canada in the field of foreign affairs can be expressed by two propositions. The first one, a positive proposition, is to promote understanding between all the nations and the second, a negative one, is to prevent armed conflicts and to maintain peace which is essential to the well-being of all nations.
The promotion of understanding between nations is quite in line with our belief that the state must serve the individual and not the other way around. It is in accordance with this principle, Mr. Speaker, that we have gradually come to reject the idea that international conflicts must be settled by force and by war. It is also that philosophy which made us realize the interdependence of nations and, as a consequence, the responsibility of the haves to help the have-nots.

External Affairs
Thus, Mr. Speaker, through the Colombo plan, through similar organizations within the United Nations and through the British Commonwealth oi nations, Canada has given help to underdeveloped or economically weak countries and has continued gradually to evolve a policy of assistance to those countries. In fact, I was glad to hear this morning the Secretary of State for External Affairs refer to the gratifying results of this policy of support, of understanding and of assistance to weaker and needier nations. It is a policy of the utmost importance, one that yields better dividends, because it is calculated to ensure world peace.
However, foreign policy aimed at preventing armed conflicts runs into more serious difficulties. It becomes so much more of a problem, due to the fact that our philosophy -and I mean the philosophy of Canada as well as that of other free nations-conflicts with that of the communist countries and their satellites.
But, Mr. Speaker, whether we profess our own philosophy or that of communist countries, the progress achieved in the field of nuclear weapons forces us to extreme caution in the field of international relations, precisely because of that danger, the possibility of a nuclear war.
Undoubtedly, the small conflicts arising here and there could lead to a conflict which might mean world destruction.
The current crisis in the Middle East is extremely serious. It illustrates this ideological conflict between free nations and communist nations. Even if it is not just like the one we had in 1956-and I agree with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) that it is not of the same nature-I believe that both crises have resulted from the same cause and that the one led to the other. It remains, Mr. Speaker, that the situation in the Middle East is not serious simply because American troops have landed in Lebanon or because British troops are posted in Jordan, nor because there was a revolution in Iraq. It is serious mainly because all those events stem from the very strength of Arab nationalism which began to develop since the rise to power of Colonel Nasser in Egypt.
In itself, that surge of Arab nationalism would not be as threatening as it is, were it not that communist countries are using it as a pretext to move in and to substitute their influence in the Middle East to the traditional influence of France, Great Britain and the United States.
At the time of the Suez conflict, it was possible to confine that outbreak by creating a United Nations force but that force which was sent to Egypt, did not constitute an

adequate solution and no doubt, at that time, great hopes were entertained that the crisis had definitely been settled. It was indeed the opinion of the Leader of the Opposition who said on March 15, 1957, I am quoting from page 2351 of Hansard:
This Middle East problem has been almost continuously before the United Nations assembly since I spoke to this house on external affairs last November and that consideration by the United Nations I think has helped not only to bring the fighting to an end in that area but to prevent the conflict breaking out again or, even worse, spreading.
However, at that time there were reasons to fear that this first conflict might spread and break out elsewhere. May I be allowed to quote a statement made at the time by the then leader of the opposition, now the Prime Minister, in reply to the secretary of state for external affairs, as reported on page 2371 of Hansard. He said:
First, we said that if necessary we should extend the United Nations police action to cover not only the borders between Egypt and Israel but also the borders between Israel and Lebanon, Syria and Jordan, because we believe it is of the greatest importance that peace must be maintained in that area. We asked that there be a peace treaty arrived at between Israel and the Arab states, and we know the extraordinary difficulties which lie in the road of that. We are convinced also that no matter how annoyed we may feel at certain individuals in the Middle East, no matter how angered we may be by their actions, it would be folly to let either annoyance or anger change us from a settled course. This course must be to secure a settlement in that area, through peace treaties arrived at between the opposing countries.
Now, precisely because the United Nations, at the time, failed to consider settlement of the whole problem, Arab nationalism, abetted by Russia, broke out once more, this time by way of indirect aggression. It is in the face of this indirect aggression, somewhat reminiscent of what happened before world war II, that the role of the United Nations organization becomes most ticklish.
We are a long way from the scene but surely we must be interested in the solution of this problem because today, the interdependence of free nations is an acknowledged fact. In the face of this difficult situation, what has been the policy of Canada and on what principles was it based?
Mr. Speaker, I think that it would not be hard to prove that our attitude in those circumstances has been consistent with our philosophy which rejects the settlement of conflicts by force. We have demonstrated our confidence in the United Nations. However, the United Nations is no stronger than its moral authority which, in turn, depends upon the support of all member nations. We know that this moral authority can fail when one or two great powers withhold their support

and also because, too often, the United Nations cannot apply in a practical way the authority it holds from the majority of its members. And 1 do believe that, if it were possible to solve the technical and practical problems involved, it would be an ideal solution to put a permanent force at the disposal of the United Nations. However, in such circumstances, there would still remain the difficulty of deciding at what time, in case of indirect aggression, this permanent force should step in.
As far as Canada is concerned, it seems to me that our policy should first be determined on the basis of unity of thought.
It is essential that we work out our international policy first on a non-partisan basis, seeking unity of thought within our country. And I believe that, in this field, the present government has continued to apply the principles applied by the former government, seeking the unity of all men of good will in the determination of our policy. I was glad to hear, last Monday, the Prime Minister thanking the Leader of the Opposition for a suggestion he had made, inviting all hon. members to present theirs and assuring them that any of their suggestions would be seriously considered by the government.
Not only should we endeavour to achieve unity of thought throughout the country, but we should also strive to achieve the same unity of thought with our allies, within the British commonwealth and the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. The British commonwealth, as a result of the diversity of nations which it includes and the diversity of economic interests of these various nations, is a body through which it is possible to work efficiently in favour of peace and understanding between nations. Within the commonwealth, precisely on account of Canada's action to which I referred a moment ago, we contribute, I think, towards greater understanding between peoples of all parts of the world. If within this organization we do achieve some unity of thought in the working out of our foreign policy, I am sure that in the United Nations we shall carry more authority over other member nations. And the situation is almost the same with regard to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization which is, of course, a defence organization. However, the latest developments, in my opinion, call for more frequent consultation between all nations belonging to that organ-
External Affairs
ization, in order that no unilateral action may be taken, and in order that any decision taken by one member of that body may be communicated to and approved by the others, in advance. In fact, here as well as abroad, we must promote understanding, we must try to understand others and make them understand our point of view.
Secondly, Mr. Speaker, I believe that our international policy must be realistic. It must be based on facts. Let us be guided by principles, but those principles must be applied to individual facts in all cases. Of course we have reached full nationhood, we are in a position to hammer out our own international policy, and we are doing just that. It would be naive to contend that our decisions are merely dictated by a feeling of subservience to Great Britain or the United States.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, since reality prevents us from taking decisions based on sentimentality, the danger at the present time is rather that, due to our economic interdependence with the United States, we might be inclined to submit to their dictates.
On the other hand, even if we have reached our maturity, we should harbour no illusion as to our ability to prevent conflicts.
Canada should not repeat the mistake of the frog that would bloat itself bigger than the ox.
It is important, Mr. Speaker, that we realize that our role should be that of a mediator, of a go-between and arbiter within the British commonwealth of nations and within NATO. If we succeed in being accepted as conciliator and mediator within these two organizations, I believe that we stand a much better chance of commanding respect for our views at United Nations. I repeat, it is important that we fully realize that ours must be a personal role, but it is also important that we do not overdo it. As long as we have a proper understanding of this role, and if we are content with it, Canada, in my opinion, will be in a better position to contribute to world peace and to the well-being of nations.
