speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a real pleasure to be able to have an opportunity to say a word about this subject which has evoked such great interest not only in the House of Commons but in this country. I think we have all been

External Affairs
much impressed in the last few days to have witnessed a part of the drama of parliament. In those recent days which were more tense than the present the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) made his statements on the international situation and we saw evidence of a high level of mature bi-partisanship in the very friendly relationship that existed between him and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson). I am sure we were all cheered and perhaps even a little thrilled by the drama of this wonderful democratic system of parliament.
I believe, too, that all Canadians followed with much interest and great pride the activities and actions of our distinguished Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Smith) as he represented Canada-and indeed, I am sure, at many times he spoke for a certain part of the free world-in these delicate and extremely important conversations which were held in the country to the south of us last week. We are proud of him, Canada is proud of him, and rightly and justly so. This is not the first crisis to stir the Canadian parliament and to interest and arouse the people of Canada and I am sure it will not be the last.
It has been said, and it is all too sadly true, that tensions today are normal. We move from crisis to crisis. We fear perhaps that one will become an explosion with catastrophic and universal effects. Happily, I believe, we live in a world which despite all its disadvantages in this connection at least has this advantage, and that is, the boiling point is higher today than it was some years ago. The nations tolerate and accept incidents which in an earlier period would have evoked a war-like response. Although the potential for destruction is greater than before, the tolerance of the nations today at least allows for a freedom of manoeuvre-ability into which our statesmanship and diplomacy may flow.
It is perhaps wrong in a general debate of this kind to concentrate all our attention on recent events in one portion of the world. Therefore perhaps I might seek in a few words to present my point of view-I am proud and happy to belong to a party which allows a backbencher to express his point of view and listens to it-on a subject so important as the relationship of some of the immediate events with the general pattern of world diplomacy.
[Mr. Macquarrie.l
The whole picture of diplomacy has changed. I can remember studying geography much less than a half century ago and at that time we learned about the great powers. I think there were seven in my day. Most of them were European and certainly the great burden of responsibility rested on the continent of Europe. We used to see an arrangement of power alignments among various members of the group of great powers. For a long time that situation prevailed and the responsibility for world peace was primarily that of Europe. Throughout the outreaches of the world the great stabilizing power of the British navy was ever-present.
Those calmer, quieter days are gone forever. We now have a situation in which two leading super-powers-one quite non-European and the other as much Asiatic as European-loom on the horizon of international affairs. The relationships between these two powers in all parts of the world form an essential part of every equation in the consideration of diplomatic questions because whether we like it or not we must accept the fact that the diplomatic interests of the U.S.S.R. and of the U.S.A. are worldwide. In recent times we have seen occasions when the interests of these two great powers have come into conflict and at some times in certain sensitive areas on the periphery of soviet power we have encountered threats that were very serious, just as threatening and dangerous as the situation through which we are now passing.
We can remember shortly after the conclusion of the second world war the problem of Iran. Then, we remember also when it was in northern Greece that the two worlds were in contact, in unhappy and bloody contact. Then, it was Korea and before that it was Berlin. I remember that over the Berlin blockade there was great danger and great anxiety, and it was the masterly display of united power that brought about a solution of that very grave situation.
Then, another place was Indo-China where the two worlds met and some kind of accommodation was necessary. I suppose a very simple illustration would be for one to look at a map of the world which we see in 1958 and compare it with one for 1938. If we did that we would see one fundamental effect of diplomatic life, and that is the tremendous spatial expansion of the Soviet union. Its growth, its extension, has been phenomenal.

We remember, too, that at one time the United States had a policy which was called a policy of containment and we used to speak about the Truman doctrine. I am one of those who still believes that the doctrine of containment was a good doctrine and that the Truman policy was a good, sound and very effective policy for dealing with the new situation which had then developed. The Berlin airlift was an expression of that and was one of the great triumphs of the western world when in unity, dignity and strength we stood by our position and we won. It is very easy-and I find a great tendency in Canada to do this-to criticize the errors, the miscalculations and the blunders of the United States in recent times in the field of foreign policy. But I think it is essential for us as an ally of the United States to consider at all times some of the difficulties and some of the realities of its position and therefore of ours.
The role of the western world has been essentially defensive. We have allowed the initiative-because we had to-to lie with the Soviet union, so we never knew just where on this great area of contact the excesses of tension would break out. At the same time it requires massive power on the part of the United States to stand ever-prepared for such a situation. It also requires great efforts on the part of the United States to bring together alliances of friends in strategic areas as an important development of its own military might. Much of the activity of the United States in the last 10 years has been in the development of those two arms of defence.
The magnitude of the responsibility of the leader of the western world has been immense. There is one that I think it is proper for a group of parliamentarians to consider. It is this, that in its diplomacy the western world must operate in the framework of popular democracy and always with regard for the moral content of our diplomatic values. We can never, in our part of the world, judge any action in purely strategic or military terms.
A few years ago there was a suggestion, which never was a very serious one, that the United States, for strategic reasons, should launch a preventive war. Whether or not, even in the narrow strategic and military sense, that would have been feasible, it was utterly impossible with the sense of values we have; but yet it was not impossible for the Soviet union to take the action which it took in Hungary not long ago. It is not under the same moral restraints as a free country with ideals and ethics which its people insist 57071-3-170
External Affairs
upon. This cannot be forgotten. Indeed, I think it should always be remembered in our occasionally, ill-advised, perhaps sometimes ungenerous criticism.
If there is one thing I believe in, not only in the history of democracy but in the history of any political or social development, it is that it is very difficult to be dogmatic, to be certain and to be self-confident. I wish I could be as sure as some members who have spoken that the action at Suez some months ago was altogether wrong, or that I could so easily and so thoroughly condemn the attitudes of the United States and the United Kingdom when, in the first moments of flux, of uncertainty-(indeed, I think the only certain thing was that a dangerous situation existed)-and believe that that immediate action was wrong, was immoral. As I say, I cannot be sure about these things; there are too many "if's"; that we can only read back into those events in the light of the things which are possible. But, as we look forward to the summit conference, we can recognize that this, too, is a part of a continuing policy.
I am sure we all were impressed the other day when the Prime Minister referred to this country's attitude on a summit meeting and said, as reported at page 2473 of Hansard:
I still believe that no nation should or dare shut the door on any matter that offers the prospect of any solution or even a diminution of international tensions.
This attitude is not at all inconsistent with a sustained posture of strength in a determination to support and maintain the position of the western world, because the two great power agglomerations today must establish some basis of accommodation, else the prospect of the future is too awful to contemplate. Therefore, I think it shows a good perception of the existing situation that our country should take an important part in arranging for the forthcoming summit meeting.
It is not my intention to discuss the various technical arrangements or make an appraisal as to whether it would be more beneficial to hold the meeting at the United Nations or elsewhere, but I do think that the general emphasis upon the universality of the United Nations' responsibility is all to the good and I think our government and our country, for this is not a partisan matter, should be commended for its action.
The present area of tension is certainly not a new one. All down through the years, from the very early days of man's social experience, this part of the world has been a trouble spot.
It has been the meeting place of continents.
It has been the lifeline of ancient empires.

External Affairs
It has been a buffer zone between east and west, often vulnerable to attack. The rough boots of the conquering invader have perhaps been heard more times over this area than in any other part of the world.
Here again in our own time we have the same area causing universal concern. But we have here factors of tension in the situation which are somewhat unique. We have fomenting in the Middle East the heady new wine of nationalism, an expression of national feeling which was very strong in Europe a century ago and very weak in other parts of the world. But now the situation is quite different and nationalism is a potent factor in Asia and Africa. I believe this was portrayed so well by a representative of an Asian nation at the United Nations some years ago when, after discussing the splendid job of administration which had been done in his country by Great Britain, he went on to say that good government is no substitute for self-government. That attitude, that very deep-seated thinking, is something which cannot be ignored.
There are other factors that are difficult to understand in their entirety and to which it is perhaps difficult to adjust ourselves. We have not only a feeling of nationalism there but strong forces leading to some kind of union among various states whose separate existence is somewhat incongruous. Many movements like to find a prophet and the present dictator of Egypt obviously aspires to be the leader of the great movement of pan-Arabism although, it would be wrong to say that he led it or created it. Perhaps he merely appropriated it. But the ambitions of the Egyptian dictator are very clearly set out in these words in a book which he wrote:
When I consider these hundreds of millions, I emerge with a sense of the tremendous possibilities which we might realize through the co-operation of all Moslems . . . enabling them and their brothers In faith to wield power wisely and without limit.
This man is the man on the scene today, a man who has the tremendous psychological impact of this feeling behind him. Perhaps in recent years we have failed, as other speakers have mentioned, to realize fully and to appreciate the forces of nationalism in this key area. I think the efforts of the western alliance were very clear. The attempt was made to build a bridge of support right across the northern tier of the Middle East, as it was called. But this was never developed with strength and in our time we have seen the constant withdrawal of western power. The withdrawal of western power seems to delight some members but whether or not it is greeted with delight or something else it has certainly happened. France withdraws from her former mandates.

Britain departs from the Suez and Sudan. She forsakes Palestine. Then into this vacuum of power comes indirect Russian power and the highly activated development of nationalism.
One hon. member has pointed out that it must be recognized that the Soviet union has interests in the Middle East. Russia has had interests in the Middle East for many years and no one denies that. Indeed Russian interest was a very definite part of the strategy and diplomacy of that period. Fifty years ago Great Britain and Russia made an arrangement as to sphere of influence in Persia. One of the agreements among those many unhappy agreements before the first world war dealt with the realization of an old Russian dream, control of Constantinople. If we remember the Victorian era, the great emphasis in British foreign policy at that time was on the containment and curtailment of Russian penetration into the Middle East. We might recall one figure who was identified with that policy, that great statesman Benjamin Disraeli.
The Middle East for over 2,000 miles bounds upon the territory of Russia or of her satellites or her allies. Her interest there is very great and she is pursuing it with all the means at her disposal, nonetheless significant or effective because often indirect.
In the Middle East we find that one of the old factors in the equation has been removed, and that is the traditional friendship between Arabs and Britons. It is a long story and it is not altogether a happy story. There were many misunderstandings, some broken promises, some agreements which perhaps should never have been made and others which perhaps should never have been broken. But in any case that old friendship is gone and it can no longer be relied upon when we consider this part of the world and this portion of the diplomatic equation.
It is always a part, of course, of every country's foreign policy to accommodate itself to new conditions. We cannot now deny the fact of Arab nationalism. Nor can we deny the fact of what is called Nasserism. It is too late to cast recriminations as to how Nasserism was created or how it was fostered. I quite agree with the hon. gentleman who declared that we must, in following our policies in this area, have reference to the interests, needs and desires of the millions of people living there. I think that in the long run that will be in our interests too.
The Leader of the Opposition and the Secretary of State for External Affairs were profoundly right when they pointed out that beyond this immediate crisis there is great urgency and great need for long-range consideration as to what will be done about the

Middle East. The western record there in recent years has not been a glorious one. We have suffered reverses. There is more that we can do and we must take the initiative. We in Canada are proud of the fact-I hope it is a wholesome and not a smug pride and I think it is the former-that we do not have a legacy of ill will there, that we are not suspect. We say that our record is good. That being the case, I think it behooves us to take more responsibility.
I have been impressed in recent years how, with the development of Canadian diplomatic posts across the world, we seem to have been so neglectful of the Middle East. There were areas there in which we should have had more highly developed listening posts than we did have. I think we could have used our position to better advantage. We could make use of our reservoir of good will and our recognition of the importance of the economic question.
We have confidence, I think, in the immediate developments. We listened with great interest as the Secretary of State for External Affairs recounted the steps which the United Nations were to take. We will follow with interest the activities of UNOGIL. However, none of these things can ever be regarded as in any way a permanent solution to the problems. Our country has not been very long in this field of foreign policy. It is only a few years, historically speaking, since Sir Robert Borden won for us a place in the international field, so to speak. We have been doing rather well, but I am sure that the challenges before us will be ever greater. I am confident that, aware of the responsibilities which we have, our response to them will be fuller, more complete, than ever before.
I hope that we will never forget that, differ as we may in the details amongst the members of the western alliance, and using our influence as we might to try to persuade the policies of those who are stronger than we are, the greatest folly of all would be to contribute in any way to the weakening of the basic unity which must exist between members of the western alliance. If there was one thing which was more disturbing than anything else in the recent Suez crisis it was the fact that there appeared to be a weakening of that essential unity which must exist between members of a free alliance dedicated to the same principles, principles which we must pursue with vigour and determination in these very tense days.

speechtext:
It is
a fortunate circumstance, Mr. Speaker, that makes it possible for me to participate in this debate following the distinguished member from Prince Edward Island who has just
57071-3-170J
External Affairs
spoken. It is not the first time I have heard him speak on the very important subject of external affairs, because just a few years ago we were more or less linked in a common interest in these matters out in my own city of Brandon. I am sure the members of the house would agree that his contribution has been enlightening and helpful this afternoon.
I have been impressed during this discussion with the unanimity that appeared on all sides. Every member who has contributed to this discussion so far has joined in agreeing that during the past few days we have been faced with the most critical situation that has confronted the world since the end of world war II, in the events that have transpired in the Middle East. I am not going to endeavour to look at this problem from the standpoint of praise and blame. I was impressed the other day, as I listened to the distinguished Prime Minister for Ghana, who I thought made an excellent contribution to the whole approach to foreign affairs, when he said he was not going to pass any judgment. It would be foolish, and it would be premature, because we are dealing with matters that are so complex that only the Almighty himself could understand actually what has transpired and what might inevitably result therefrom.
There has been the common reaction that we, in this chamber, have been deeply disturbed and troubled by the events. I think the general feeling that has gone across the country has been that we have been hovering in the shadow of a possible outbreak of world war III. Perhaps one of the reasons for such a deeply troubled feeling in the country is that these events are taking place in the Middle East. The Middle East is generally regarded as the cradle of civilization, as it is from that area that the three great western religions have had their source, Judaism, Moslemism and Christianity. Yet, notwithstanding the historic past in this part of the world, it has almost seemed in recent years that what we have regarded as the cradle of civilization might become, unless we are very careful and unless we are very wise in the way we handle this problem, the grave of civilization. I believe that is the spirit that has been present in this discussion this afternoon and is the universal attitude in regard to these matters. Mankind has the feeling that he lies under the threat of universal Hiroshima.
Of course, the Middle East problem is not the only trouble spot in the modern world. Like the previous speaker, I feel we in this mid-twentieth century period have almost become accustomed to living from crisis to crisis. It is these circumstances that arise which add to the confusion of the twentieth

External Affairs
century in which we have seen social and political change move forward at such tremendous speed it has been quite impossible for the mind of man to keep abreast, and certainly it has been impossible for our social institutions to keep up with these changes.
In every generation, the record of history tells us that there are times of social change and social confusion. In fact, if we were to go back to the beginning of the record in scripture, we would find in the opening verses of the Book of Genesis a description of the beginning of things which would tell us that the pattern that has unfolded since that time has been typical of the situation in human affairs. We are told that in the beginning God created the world. Then, the words go on to say:
And the earth was without form, and void; and darkness was upon the face of the deep.
Finally, we are given a ray of hope:
And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters.
And God said, let there be light: and there was light.
In that second verse I think we have a very apt description of the situation confronting those of us in the twentieth century, namely that the affairs of men are without form and void and darkness is brooding over the face of the earth. The events of recent days and of recent years have definitely demonstrated that there is continuing chaos and confusion.
It has been my privilege, Mr. Speaker, since I came into this house, to take part in several debates on external affairs. I have done so only infrequently because these matters deal with complex matters that cannot be discussed without considerable thought and consideration. I remember the discussions that revolved around Canada's participation in NATO. I remember the heart searching there was when we were considering the proposal of German rearmament and German participation in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. At that time it was thought that here was the main trouble-spot in the world and that here would be the possible source in the future of any serious outbreak of hostilities. It might be that such is still the case because we are still confronted with the very vexing problem of German reunification. I agreed entirely with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) when he emphasized that we should not forget the role of the NATO nations during the present crisis, and that is something we must continually keep in the back of our minds.
Then the trouble-spot moved towards the Far East to Korea, Formosa, Indo-China and all those other areas that have marked the

headlines of our newspapers during the years that have gone by in the recent past. We thought that there might be the final source of the outbreak of hostilities which is universally dreaded by mankind everywhere. But now attention has been focused on the situation in the Middle East. As a result of the Suez event, and as a result of the continuing difficulties on the Israeli frontier I sometimes feel that we are forced to the conclusion that today the way to Washington and Ottawa and London may be through New Delhi and Cairo.
It seems to me that a new power situation has emerged in the world or at least has become clarified. The trends have been there for some time but it is only in recent years that these trends have emerged in a distinctive form. I refer to the awakening of the underdeveloped countries in Asia and Africa, their demands for independence and selfgovernment and the rising claim of the coloured races to their share of the world's goods.
As I look at the situation, Mr. Speaker, and as I have seen the pendulum of the threat of war swing from Europe to the Far East and now to the Middle East, I am almost forced to the conclusion that this awakening of the peoples of Africa and Asia is a more significant development than even the events of world war I and world war II and even more significant than the rise and fall of Hitler and nazism or the Russian revolution. As a result of these new forces in world affairs we are no longer faced with the power situation that confronted us immediately following the war. I refer to the so-called east-west bloc with the west on one side of the chasm and the east on the other, the west led by the United States of America and the east led by the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, separated by the unbridgeable chasm in world affairs since the end of world war II.
But now in the world we have this new situation-we might almost call it a third force-the tremendous political power of the upsurge of nationalism in the underdeveloped countries and their increasing desire and demands for a place in the sun. These nations are largely the smaller neutral nations. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that they are exerting and are going to exert in the future an influence to which we in the west must pay increasing attention.
I say that this force represents a neutral force because as I have examined the situation and as I have listened to spokesmen and as I met some of those spokesmen here is what I found. Judging from their statements and their comments, they have no particular

desire to be drawn in the direction of either the western orbit or the eastern orbit. That point was underlined by the prime minister of Ghana when he spoke in this house the other morning. I merely quote his words to emphasize that point. He spoke of a positive neutralism. As the Hansard record reveals it, he said this:
I should like to take this opportunity to comment on certain aspects of our foreign policy. Basically the policy of our government is one of non-alignment and positive neutrality. I have emphasized on several occasions, however, that this should not be interpreted as a purely negative neutralism. On the contrary, we will always adopt whatever positive policy will do most to safeguard our independence. We have a vested interest in peace, and we will do everything in our power to support the United Nations.
I think we make a mistake, Mr. Speaker, if we regard the cause, so far as our relationships with these new uncommitted countries are concerned, as a lost cause. Out of the present disturbance in the Middle East I am optimistic enough to believe that there yet will come a new and more positive approach to these difficulties. Actually I suppose that the real motivation in the thinking of these neutral powers today is their mortal fear of the military force concentrated in the so-called civilized nations of the east and of the west.
In this debate so far it seems to me that the shadow of the Suez crisis has been hovering near. In his remarks the Leader of the Opposition made some reference to this matter this afternoon. It is true that there are certain similarities that can be noted in reference to the Suez crisis and the present difficulty. It was a manifestation of anticolonialism which is peculiar to these neutral nations.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at the supper hour I had been dealing with what I regard as a very important development in the power structure of international affairs and pointing out that no longer is a two-power world a valid concept. 1 mean by that the old east-west motion of power politics that prevailed after world war II. It seems to me that the rising influence of the neutral, uncommitted nations is the most significant development in international affairs in recent times. They have the legitimate desire to strive for a place in the sun.
As I understand the problem of the Middle East it would certainly appear that in the background, at least as the basic motivating force, is this desire for self-government, for independence, for a place in the sun on the part of an increasing number of underdeveloped regions. The Middle East situation has been at the boiling point for some years. As the house rose I was making a comparison with the events that took place at the time of the Suez crisis-this was referred to by the Leader of the Opposition this afternoon-

and was about to comment that in those events we can trace the growing wave of anti-colonialism.
I recall, for example, during the last war when I had the privilege of being in the Middle East in the uniform of the Royal Canadian Air Force that even as far back as 18 years ago that underlying hostility to the west could be felt on all sides. It is also significant that the mere fact that I and other Canadian servicemen were wearing the Canada badge at that time caused us to be regarded with special respect by the people in the city of Cairo, where we had contact from time to time during our visits to that area.
That spirit of anti-colonialism is present today in much greater intensity. It is generated by this striving toward nationalism. Certainly it has been encouraged by a political figure such as Nasser but it would be present even had Colonel Nasser not risen to a position of influence in the Middle East at the present time. Some one has said that no matter what attempts are made to the contrary, under the upsurge of interest in the United Arab Republic, federation will take place regardless of other considerations.
At the time of the Suez situation there was a fundamental difference from the condition prevailing at the moment. There was an unfortunate confusion and division in policy amongst the nations of the west. This prevailed in both the NATO countries and the countries of the commonwealth. To my mind that was the most unhappy aspect of the whole Suez crisis. I felt at the time, and I stated in the debate that took place on that occasion, that Britain's withdrawal from the Middle East would leave a power vacuum that was bound to create even greater trouble in the future. There is not a doubt in the world but that the present machinations there have been intensified and facilitated by the departure of British influence from that area. I believe this point was made this afternoon by the Leader of the Opposition, and I thought it was rather speculative, that if Britain had not gone through with its intervention in that area in that particular incident then Nasser would have been crushed by the Israeli forces. My understanding of the British intervention at that time was that it was a desire to stop hostilities in the fear that their continuation might precipitate a third world war which is feared so much in all parts of the world.
There is a very much happier note in the crisis we are facing today. There is a spirit of unity of purpose and unity of policy amongst the commonwealth nations as well as amongst the nations participating in the
External Affairs
North Atlantic Treaty Organization. I should like to express a word of appreciation at this time to both the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Smith) for the important part they have played in making possible this present spirit of unanimity amongst the nations of the west. They have exerted initiative in exactly the right amount and at precisely the correct moment to make it possible for the western forces to rally around a common meeting point. In so doing for the first time Canada is beginning to enter into that long-desired role where she is initiating policy of her own rather than being a mere echo of either the British viewpoint or the viewpoint of our neighbour to the south, the United States of America.
It is a happy state of affairs when we see the commonwealth and western nations working together in a unity never achieved before to meet a common crisis. It goes without saying, too that we are all delighted that this problem is finding its way back to the United Nations and that the prestige of the United Nations is not being undermined by any attempt to institute deliberations outside the framework of that organization. A large part of the credit for the initiative in this regard, I feel, goes to the Prime Minister and our Secretary of State for External Affairs.
Having said that much about the note of unanimity I must add a further word concerning the general approach to the problem confronting us. It seems that the concept of power politics is still the basic approach of the west to the settling of these disturbed conditions. The very fact that we have had to adopt at least military acts by landing troops in the trouble area is a confession of our own failure to grasp the essential nature of the problem and to try to reconcile this growing spirit of nationalism with the interests of the western nations in the Middle Eastern area.
It does not need any emphasizing to make the point that in this hydrogen age it is no longer possible to maintain the balance of power by means of the old power politics idea. It is much too dangerous a balance to try to resolve on that basis. That is why it is so disturbing when we read remarks by the premier of the soviets as quoted in an editorial of the Globe and Mail today, as follows:
Let the imperialists beware. We are revolutionaries. We are Marxists and we are delighted when the colonial nations rise up and cast off their chains. The boot of the foreigner must be removed from their soil.
That is not the kind of attitude that is going to bring about the necessary reconciliation of viewpoint and interests at this time. There had been an encouraging indication,

External Affairs
particularly since 1956, that the Russian emphasis on power politics, the effectiveness of power politics in the world struggle had diminished somewhat. They seemed to be backing away from a brutal power concept. For example, they had minimized somewhat their stress of the theory of the inevitability of war in achieving desired ends, and also there seemed to be a softening of belief in the necessity for civil war for the seizure of power in any outside nation. More recently, too, there has been the tendency to emphasize the economic struggle rather than the political or the military struggle. It is to be hoped that spokesmen of the U.S.S.R., when they come together in the contemplated summit conference, will adopt a much milder tone than in the statement that was released by the Russian premier in response to the statement of the President of the United States of America.
I cannot get out of my mind that in the background somewhere in the thinking of the soviets there might be mischief contemplated and I still remember the quotation of Premier Khrushchev when he said /'Always remember that the bear can crush just as effectively with a hug as it can with a blow." That is provocative language and it is language that should not be used if we are to have any success at all in the summit conference.
I say that the old concept of power politics is outmoded by the very nature of the world in which we live. We could not keep up to the soviet in adopting this technique even if we tried. The Minister of External Affairs (Mr. Smith) referred to the subtle intervention penetration of the soviets and the difficulty of analysing the nature of this subtlety. That is quite true. A monolithic state such as the soviets is always at an advantage in this regard. There are no democratic inhibitions, no rules to follow, and on top of it there is the strong outthrust in the cold war of communism as a new world religion. We just cannot compete in the same league with that kind of approach.
I feel, Mr. Speaker, that our approach at this time-and I am sure the sharp reaction of all the leaders of the west indicates that they realize the difficulty-toward a solution of the problem must be other than that of the outmoded power politics. Already we have made very remarkable forward steps in this regard, and I refer now to the attempts of the west to provide economic assistance to those under-developed areas in a gesture of good will and of understanding. It is a great step forward when we reach the point that we are more and more interested in

offering economic aid than we are in providing military aid to assist those new and developing neutral nations.
I could spend some time this evening, were time available, in analysing the role that oil plays in the present problem of the Middle East. There is not the time but I think we are aware that if we are to avoid further alienation of the neutral nations we must make it quite certain that we have only their best interests at heart, that we want to assist them in every way to achieve their legitimate desires for independence and self-government.
My final point, Mr. Speaker, is perhaps the main point that I wish to bring before the house tonight. It deals further with this subtle approach, this subtle intervention that is the growing influence in world affairs at the present time. I refer to the impact of psychological warfare, the psychological factors in the cold war, the role that values play in influencing world events. At the time of Suez the United States prided itself on the fact that it had struck the correct moral tone in its approach to that problem and condemnation was heaped upon Britain and France because they had acted independently of the United Nations, outside the moral framework of our Christian ethic. Well, as far as that went at the time I could agree with the United States postulate. It is very important that we exert a proper moral leadership. The difficulty was that having, as they claimed to have, achieved a position of prestige and world leadership in the Middle East, the United States did not move fast enough to consolidate that position.
We always have to look at these problems from two standpoints, the standpoint of political realism as well as the standpoint of idealism. We in the west are essentially idealistic. The Americans and Canadians are particularly idealistic but I am afraid there are times that our idealism is so badly adulterated by materialism that we cannot see the woods for the trees, as it were. President Eisenhower has said that in the end result there is very little difference between atheistic materialism and theistic materialism. The soviet system is quite unashamedly materialistic.
They believe in the efficacy of physical power, prowess and military force. We have depended upon these things only because we have felt ourselves forced by outside pressures and threats.
Yet as a theistic society, we too have become saturated by theistic materialism. Our symbols of democracy, those things that we would wish to bring before people who in the first instance actually receive their inspiration from the west through our missionaries, our religious missionaries, our

church missionaries, our political emissaries, our commercial salesmen, have been contused by these people with such physical achievements as skyscrapers, juke boxes, refrigerators and the like. Sometimes too it seems to me that the symbols of democracy are obscured completely by the very struggle for existence of these underdeveloped nations.
A truism that used to be preached by General Booth of the Salvation Army was that you cannot preach to a man with an empty stomach. I am quite sure that we cannot expect these nations, with their low standard of living and faced with very difficult economic circumstances, to understand our democratic ideas as long as all their time is consumed in the task of eking out a bare existence.
My time is expiring, Mr. Speaker, and I must bring these remarks to a close. I think we are in a much happier position in the present crisis than we were at the time of Suez. Canada has added laurels to the lustre that is already ours because of our participation in world affairs down through the years. The Prime Minister of Ghana paid us a generous tribute in speaking in the house last Monday when he said that he was greatly impressed by Canada's record in the field of international affairs in recent years. I believe firmly that at the summit conference and out of the present discussions and deliberations we will see a coming together of the leaders of the various nations of the world, a closer understanding of the basic issues and an attempt to get at the common humanities underlying the skin of each one of us. If we get the other man's point of view I think we can go a long way in helping to resolve the problem.
Mr. Speaker, I recall an interesting discussion at the United Nations in the fall of 1955. The very delicate and difficult race problem in South Africa was under discussion. I remember that the representative of Indonesia was speaking. He said that the white man believes that the only solution for the problem of South Africa is for all blacks to turn white. With a smile and with a good natured chuckle he went on to say, "I have got another solution for the problem. Why should not all white men turn black?" You see Sir it all depends how you look at the situation.
We have many problems to contend with but I think the basic solution is that we interpret correctly our way of life, the values underlying our way of life. As the United Nations charter so ably puts it, if wars begin in the minds of men it is in the minds and hearts of men that the defences of peace must be built. Canada has made a great
External Affairs
contribution to that great structure in the past and will make even greater contributions in the critical days that lie immediately ahead.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the debate that has taken place on the resolution proposed today by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Smith) represents the common desire of all of us in the house to assist the government in the very difficult responsibilities confronting it at this time. At the same time each of us is anxious to bring forward views that we believe are directed towards that particular objective. We may not all agree on the details of foreign policy of the government of our country but I am sure that all of us in the house without exception are united by a common purpose on a common understanding of the difficult problems involved and confronting each country in the world at this particular moment.
Like my leader I should like to say to the Secretary of State for External Affairs that we on this side of the house, free from direct responsibility, extend to him, to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and to the other members of the government our best wishes for a satisfactory discharge of their responsibilities in respect of these matters, some of which in other days have engaged the attention of some who have spoken today. Possibly in my case I can say to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, remembering the period when I did have a status best described by saying that I was in statu pupillari, that I have for him nothing but best wishes in the discharge of responsibilities which are his for some months.
I echo at once the words of my leader who expressed his faith in the United Nations and in its charter. As one who has spent a good part of his life in a less effective way at the league of nations and at the United Nations, I feel that it is well that we should have had today, through one who has played such a great part in current events in our time, an expression of faith in the value of the charter and in the concept of collective security as a means of bringing about order in a disturbed world. I am sure that hon. gentlemen opposite will not begrudge me this opportunity to say that. We have been proud of my leader in his former capacity of secretary of state for external affairs and as a great exponent of peace in our time. But we thought today that in the bold initiative he took in his speech he lived up in an exceptional way to the high standards which he has set for himself in this important field of human endeavour.
He began his speech by suggesting to the Secretary of State for External Affairs that

External Affairs
as the general assembly would meet in normal session some time in the month of September, consideration might be given by the Canadian delegation to a strong sponsorship and initiative regarding certain matters that have a bearing on whether or not we are going to be able to ease current international tension and make a contribution in a positive way to the preservation of peace in the world.
He suggested we might take the initiative at the assembly in the matter of trying to bring about some agreement that would lead to the arresting or stopping of the manufacture of nuclear weapons, now confined to three powers; that secondly, we might put forward in a way acceptable to a wide number of nations an agreement that would lead to the suspension of tests, he suggested for a period of five years, under the supervision of the United Nations; and, thirdly, echoing one of his favourite themes, he urged that in the face of the current international situation we might find great encouragement for pressing forward with the establishment of a permanent United Nations police force.
I am sure that all members on all sides of the house, including the Prime Minister, whose interest in this matter was represented by the interrogation he levelled at the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), will agree, at least in principle, that the principle of collective security as envisaged by its authors at San Francisco can be effectively realized by the acceptance of an additional principle of collective security and by doing indirectly what it has not been possible to do directly because of the intransigence of the Soviet union in respect of the implementation of article 43 of the charter of the United Nations. Whether or not it is possible to establish a permanent United Nations police force remains to be seen. But undoubtedly, if we are to pursue the original concept of the interdependence of the nations of the world as envisaged by Her Majesty's Prime Minister in the United Kingdom, this is the next phase towards which we must seek to develop the principle of collective security, attempted in 1919 in the covenant and so unfortunately rejected Anally in September of 1939 by so many members of the league of nations.
Then, my leader spoke of the importance of initiative, not irresponsible initiative but initiative on the part of nations who have won respect of their fellow members in the United Nations, capable of providing constructive solutions for difficult problems. Possibly no one had a greater right to suggest that we should pursue this tactic of initiative than my leader, who perhaps more than any other man in the last decade, has day in and

day out at the United Nations himself given an example of what responsible initiative can mean towards the achievement of good purposes amongst the nations. He expressed the views, and I think we all associate ourselves with this, that we are proud of the role of Canada in recent days. This does not mean that every particular act of the administration commends itself to us. Indeed, speaking for myself, it would be possible to argue that in the Arst few hours of this current situation there might be found occasion for justiAable wonder as to the actual course that the government of our country had in mind.
Whether or not that is right, the fact is that subsequent events, declarations of the Prime Minister in this house, statements of the Secretary of State for External Affairs at the United Nations, the reported meetings that he has had with his opposite number in the United Kingdom and the United States, all suggest that the role of Canada in the past few days has been such as to warrant the observation of my leader that we approve in a general way the role of Canada in these recent days. However, I wonder why the Secretary of State for External Affairs, when he spoke today about meetings in Washington on Friday of last week with Mr. Dulles and with Mr. Selwyn Lloyd, referred to the reports made in the United States press as to the nature of Canada's contribution. It may be that because negotiations on these matters sometimes obviously must be private at certain stages he could go no further. But it would have been helpful, assuming that under the circumstances it would have been desirable for him to do so, to have an account from him of precisely the position that Canada took in the conversations that were held at that time, prior to the conversation he had the following day on this crisis with the secretary general of the United Nations.
We had today from my leader, I think, a valuable historical statement of the situation in the Middle East, a historical narrative that puts its problems in prospective. Then, associated with that, was the concrete proposal made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs who spoke Arst. Speaking of the situation historically in the Middle East, my leader mentioned the constant strife that has prevailed in that theatre, without attributing to any particular source the cause of the strife, indicating the competitive forces that persist; the interest of the Soviet union currently and historically in the Middle East; the animosities that prevail between the various groups, and suggested that whatever kind of formula eventuates we must bear in mind these impotrant historical facts, amongst

which is the natural urge of the people of the Middle East, as well as other nations, for self-determination. We must note their desire to use whatever help they can get, from whatever quarter, to further their nationalist aspirations. We must recognize, too, that these aspirations, no matter what will happen within the next few months, are bound in the processes of human history, to assert themselves as they have asserted themselves in the past. I thought he left the implication that what we must seek to do is avoid creating any unduly lengthy breach of misunderstanding between the western nations and these nations in the Middle East.
It undoubtedly was because of considerations of this sort that the Secretary of State for External Affairs projected the idea that one way of bringing about stability in the Middle East would be to provide for some form of international guarantee of the neutrality of Lebanon. When I first heard the Secretary of State for External Affairs make this proposal, without in any way disagreeing with it, but reflecting on what it meant, I found myself hoping that the Secretary of State for External Affairs might have found it possible-he undoubtedly had his reasons for not doing so-to explain the reasons which prompted him to underline this very interesting suggestion, which I noted during the dinner hour was made in a recent issue of Le Monde.
The article in that newspaper called attention to the fact that Lebanon vis-a-vis the other nations of the Middle East for a long time has occupied a position of unofficial but acknowledged neutrality, a neutrality that was respected historically up until perhaps a year ago by the adoption of the Eisenhower doctrine, a position which the Secretary of State for External Affairs compared to the guarantee of neutrality given to Austria in the treaty of peace signed by the Soviet union and certain western powers four or five years ago.
I am sure there is much merit in the suggestion made today by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. However, I am sure that he would agree with me that the guaranteeing of the neutrality of Lebanon to preserve the national integrity of that historic little community and state could serve as a pilot project for guaranteeing the neutrality of other countries in the Middle East as well. One thinks, of course, immediately of Israel. Certainly to guarantee the integrity of Israel would be a stabilizing factor in the Middle East. But one should not even stop with Israel. Guaranteeing the neutrality of other nations of the Middle East by these nations themselves
External Affairs
and by other nations of the world might well prove to be an extremely important factor just as the neutrality of Austria in recent years has proved to be a valuable asset and as the neutrality of Switzerland for a long period now has served as an extremely useful facet in the conduct of international affairs.
I would hope that I do not misread the objectives that the government has in mind and particularly the Secretary of State for External Affairs in saying that not only would we want to guarantee the territorial and national integrity of Lebanon but we would also want to see the expansion of that principle in the wider theatre of the Middle East itself as a means of steadying and disciplining those forces that have existed and have contributed so much to the lack of order which has existed in those areas during the past decade and more. In any event, one can only hope that these suggestions will be pursued with vigour and initiative by the government of this country in the days and months ahead in order to achieve what we all so earnestly desire.
Immediately we are confronted with a proposal by which this problem in the Middle East is to be met and by which it is hoped tension can be eased not only for the benefit of this area but for other areas as well. The proposal has been made that the way in which to do this is for the heads of the governments of the great powers to confront one another and to deliberate on matters relating to the Middle East. This it is argued might have a steadying and'clarifying influence. I want to say first of all that as an individual I believe that nothing is to be lost in principle by those who have the responsibility in these matters in various countries getting to know one another in the hope that as a result of such acquaintance they will better be equipped and disposed to resolve the frightening problems that divide them. But I think we have to resort to the practice and the achievements of history in assessing whether or not this understandably good wish is practical in every circumstance. Argument, talks and articles about a summit meeting to end the cold war I think very often give one a feeling of unrealism, almost childishness, sometimes of nightmarish insincerity. The notes fly back and forth on who will meet, where, when, how, why, and with what; notes usually given to the public before they have been received by the person or the country to whom they are addressed. I think the former secretary of state for external affairs, my leader, properly

External Affairs
expressed the situation in this particular when at Williamsburg he recently said:
The best kind of summit meeting that I can visualize in present circumstances-and it would be no formal conference at all-would be a meeting of the heads of the American and Russian governments for a couple of days, without agenda, files, or crowds of experts; to exchange views informally and frankly; to try to get to understand each other and in the process perhaps to remove some misconceptions and even some fears. Then, the work of negotiation and diplomacy on a wider basis and dealing with concrete problems-the long, hard pull-could follow and in perhaps a better atmosphere.
Then he went on to say this:
The worst kind of summit conference that I can imagine is a meeting of the heads of a dozen or more governments, more or less evenly divided between communists, anticommunists and uncommitted, each with a staff of a hundred or so, and all surrounded by 4,000 journalists, photographers, radio and television commentators, crouching on any ledge they can find, however uncomfortable, providing it is on or near the summit. In this melange, there will be only one man who knows exactly what he wants to do, Mr. Khrushchev. He will submit ten propositions at once to the conference, full of such words as peace, co-existence, disarmament, prohibition, and ask that they be agreed to at once as being entirely consistent with the Sermon on the Mount and the U.N. Charter. He will have a wonderful time and the Asians, Africans and Arabs-and others-will blame everything on Mr. Dulles.
My leader has fairly good authority for this a priori view that not necessarily is related to the current suggestion that, in the face of exigencies as they are now presented, there is no alternative but to do what I think the Prime Minister so properly suggested the other day, namely that this meeting should take place. Sir Winston Churchill said as early as 1953:
This conference-
He was speaking of a summit conference.
-should not be overhung by a ponderous or rigid agenda or led into mazes and jungles of technical details, zealously contested by hordes of experts and officials drawn up in a vast cumbrous array.
The conference should be confined to the smallest number of powers and persons possible. It should meet with a measure of informality and a still greater measure of privacy and seclusion.
No one will deny that throughout the whole of his prime ministership during the period of war no one was more properly gregarious and more interested in meeting those in other countries who had to do with similar problems than was the prime minister of Great Britain. Indeed, Viscount Montgomery expressed the same view in this city only a few weeks ago when he said:
Two talking couldn't decide anything but at least they might find out what is the trouble.
In the preparations and the suggestions that the Prime Minister and his colleagues will be making about this summit meeting I think

they will want to bear in mind, as I am sure the Prime Minister is doing, the desirability of a meeting at the summit under circumstances the most practicable and in a form the most desirable to achieve the purposes that he and all others must at this time have in mind.
My leader suggested the other day when commenting on a statement made by the Prime Minister in this house and bearing in mind, undoubtedly, some of these particular situations which I have related, that a subcommittee of the security council might be devised to decide on the most effective way of bringing about what is commonly desired in this matter. This may not be possible and the Prime Minister has information, as has the Secretary of State for External Affairs, which is not available to the rest of us, but I think that this may be a valuable suggestion for the Prime Minister to bear in mind.
Assuming there is a summit conference and assuming that he will take responsibility, as head of the government of Canada, for sitting in the Canadian chair, and assuming that it should turn out-and I am not saying that this will eventuate-that the particular locale selected and the particular prearranged circumstances for the meeting prove not to be fully satisfactory, then this idea of a smaller committee could very well prove workable and it could be convoked at some subsequent date, possibly not too far removed from the date of the larger meeting but in another locale or even on another continent. This locale could be Geneva. We must not forget that in the month of July 1954 the heads of the governments of the United States, the Soviet union, France and Great Britain did meet for a week in Geneva. President Eisenhower, Premier Bulganin, Premier Faure and Mr. Eden were present and we all recall that at that meeting, when the agenda was not too carefully pre-arranged, the discussions resulted in the creation- perhaps it was a false creation but it nevertheless existed-of a measure of confidence and trust as between the four powers which had not existed for some time.
I suspect that in spite of the fact that there was a lot of publicity connected with that meeting the negotiations for the most part were held in private and it may be that this experience will prove useful when considering the events having to do with the setting up of the machinery and the decisions on the circumstances as to where and when the heads of the great powers or the members of the security council and certain other invited states shall meet. In any event, those are suggestions put forward without any background knowledge to the Prime Minister, who I know wishes to discharge, as do his

colleagues, his responsibilities in this matter in the interests of our country and in the interests of preservation of peace in the world; and as a private member of this house I give them to him.
I was very interested in what the Secretary of State for External Affairs had to say about the formula for the adjournment sine die of the international supervisory commission on control in Laos and Cambodia. These commissions, as I understand it, have now adjourned sine die-
