subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
-in Laos and in Cambodia the adjournment has yet to take place. All I can say is that even though he did not say this, it seems clear that the adjournment sine die means that the commissions will not return, certainly not to Laos; and assuming the realization of the same position in Cambodia, it will not return to Cambodia. I am not quarrelling with that; I think this is a rather ingenious solution to a problem which has concerned the government of Canada for some time.
No doubt these two commissions as well as the commission in Viet Nam have served an outstanding purpose and, as the Leader of the Opposition said today, the fact that Poland, India and Canada are represented on those commissions is possibly demonstrative of what can happen on a much wider scale in a sphere in which there would be participation by nations of both east and west which would be designed, by employing the instruments of adjudication and conciliation, to ease tension and preserve peace.
It is right that the commission in Viet Nam should continue as a means of guaranteeing satisfactory conditions for the holding of an election in that country on terms which will permit the elections to be free and so that the people of that troubled country may have the opportunity of deciding whether or not they are to follow the leadership of that great liberal-minded statesman, President Diem, or to follow the dictates of the representatives of communist China and of the Soviet union in North Viet Nam.
I also want to pay tribute to the members of the international commission in the three countries I visited a year and a half ago, not only with respect to the military personnel but also those officials of the Department of External Affairs who under great difficulties and sacrifices have rendered a very distinct service to our country and to the cause of international peace.
The Secretary of State for External AfEairs
concluded his statement with a recital of the
problems of disarmament. Of course, as my
External Affairs
leader said, disarmament could begin with the suspension of nuclear tests. This could be the beginning of a solution for a problem which has confronted the United Nations since the first meeting of that body in Church House in London, in 1946. It has not been possible to achieve any success with respect to this matter, and I fully agree with the Secretary of State for External Affairs who believes that because of the tensity of the current international situation we should not prevent a discussion of disarmament. I am not going to engage in an argument as to whether disarmament is the cause of war or whether it is a reflection of international tension, but undoubtedly the very reasons that provoked the suggestion that there should be a suspension of tests are the same kind of reasons which should provoke civilized men and women to try and bring about in their respective countries policies designed to reduce the heavy burdens of armament in a manner consistent of course with national security.
We have always made it plain in this country-and this applies to this government as well as the previous administration-in our talks with the Soviet union and with our friends the representatives of the United States, of France and of the United Kingdom, that we are not engaged in a process of trying to bring about unilateral disarmament but that we wanted disarmament on such conditions that we would be certain both sides of an agreement were carrying out the various terms to which they had committed their governments. I agree that for us not only inspection and control are important. It is also important that we have a clear understanding with the Soviet union as to what we mean by the objectives of control.
The Soviet union has traditionally taken the position that this really does not matter but that what does matter is an agreement in principle, the matter of control could be decided or discussed later. That is a chance, obviously, which in the light of the current international situation no country could take. I was a little mystified, however, when the Secretary of State for External Affairs, referring to the disarmament program as revealed in the white paper which he tabled, described it as a package deal. If by "package deal" is meant that there must be an acceptance of all its provisions, then I must say I never understood that to be the position of the previous administration nor do I understand it to be the position taken by the United States, by France or by the United Kingdom. I have always understood that we were prepared to embark on a stage by stage program insisting only at the end of each stage that

External Affairs
there would be set up the kind of international control and inspection which would guarantee the fulfilment by both sides of the features of the particular stage to which agreement in principle had been accorded.
In any event, if we have not succeeded in bringing about some progress in a measure of disarmament the fault lies at the doorstep of the Soviet union because of its reluctance to accept these elementary guarantees of control and supervision which are inherent in the character of nuclear weapons of war now in the possession of at least three of the great powers.
I hope the government will persist in this matter of disarmament, and I believe it will, no matter how frustrating it becomes and no matter how much patience it takes, remembering as the Leader of the Opposition recalled today one of his own initial participations in the field of international affairs at a disarmament conference long before the outbreak of the second world war. We all remember the long periods of discussion from 1922 on under the chairmanship of Mr. Henderson toward conditions which ultimately led to a form of unilateral disarmament which placed many nations of the free world in a disadvantageous position visa-vis Hitler's Germany. That shall not occur again, that is clear. And once the deliberations of the scientists at Geneva have been concluded, once it is determined that it is scientifically possible to supervise the suspension of these tests, it may be hoped that will be a strong stimulant for agreement in the first stages covering conventional arms and leading ultimately down to the prohibition of the manufacture and use of atomic weapons along the lines indicated by my leader this afternoon.
I fully agree with what was said about economic assistance to other countries. The role of Canada in the Colombo plan is well known. Now we have to envisage a wider form of assistance, either bilaterally or through the United Nations toward countries in the Middle East or countries already begun through the form of limited technical assistance thus far in the Caribbean and, let it not be mistaken, apart from Ghana, assistance to other theatres, including Africa itself.
This will place great obligations on the citizens of individual countries where the governments of those nations have to make policies that lead to the act of giving. That will place not only upon the people but upon those of us in political parties the responsibility of realizing that in urging these things in parliament we are in honour bound precluded from using them in inverse manner when we come to face the electorate which so often happens and has happened in this

country. The Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs may be assured that they have from us on this side of the house, as my leader said with much greater authority than I, nothing but good will and best wishes in the prosecution of their difficult responsibilities.
We are not the leading power in the world. That is a self-evident statement. But we are a nation that is respected. We are a nation which, because of the achievements in this field during the past decade, has won for itself an honoured place among the nations of the world. We have an opportunity of taking initiatives not open to every other country, not only among the smaller and middle but among the greater powers, initiatives which still rest within the power of any government of our country. Mr. Henry A. Kissinger, writing in the Ottawa Journal of May 15, 1958, said:
The more intransigent the Soviet union the more important it is for us constantly to put forward proposals which demonstrate our willingness to settle, but which also define the issue for which we are prepared to contend. We should make no proposal we are not willing to see accepted but by the same token we should not refrain from making proposals simply because we believe they may not be accepted. We are under no obligation to frame proposals we are sure the Soviet union will accept. To do so would invite the U.S.S.R. to drive us back step by step. We are under an obligation to make responsible proposals which are not designed to undermine legitimate soviet interests.
These are words to which I am sure all of us will subscribe and which I commend to the Prime Minister at this time. I take my seat by simply saying to the Prime Minister on one occasion when my leader as then secretary of state for external affairs asked me to go to the United Nations to head our delegation, the right hon. gentleman served on that delegation as an observer. He will recall our pleasant and what I think I may describe as a useful association. As I now look at him sitting in the seat-my leader said in the seats of the mighty, and it is true,- occupied by the first minister of this country, I recall that association and I know that now occupying a post of even greater responsibility than that which he occupied in 1955 the right hon. gentleman will go to the United Nations bearing in mind the tradition in the field of foreign affairs established by others and to which this house has contributed in its discussions, and he will do his utmost not only for the honour of Canada but for the peace of the world.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is indeed an occasion, one of those that occur from time to time, when this House of Commons becomes a cathedral in devotion to great principles. I am sure every hon. member of this house

was moved by the power and eloquence of the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) as he revealed his views in connection with the seriousness and in keeping with the seriousness of the situation which has been the basis of our discussion today. Indeed, from the time the debate started this afternoon one could be very proud of a House of Commons which produced the contributions that were made here as hon. members on both sides of the house spoke, beginning with the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Smith) and followed by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) in what I may be allowed to say was a masterful analysis, and finally now concluding with the speech of the hon. member for Essex East. I am not going to bring into this discussion any of those things that are past. Once or twice the Leader of the Opposition went back two years ago, almost to the crisis at the time of Suez. On this occasion I do not intend to return to those events, nor to deal with them again.
Today we are faced with a situation, and have been during the last two weeks, serious in its import, challenging in the opportunity that comes to those of us in office who have responsibility. We hope we may discharge those duties that are imposed upon us by virtue of the position we occupy in keeping with the nature of the challenge that is ours. We find, however, that there are bright sides. Today we find the United Kingdom and the United States in a degree of unity which is necessary if freedom is to be preserved. We realize something of how fearful the prospect would be if the United Kingdom, the United States and France found themselves in disagreement at a time like this.
As the hon. member for Essex East said, whatever the results of the summit conference, should it be convened-and I am implying no doubt by placing my remarks in that form-mankind and free men everywhere must never place that degree of faith in the conference which would remove the realities of the future or the realization of the fact that the division as between the forces of freedom and the communist world will still continue, not I hope in the same attitude of mind as has prevailed recently but certainly let no one carry in his heart the hope that all will be solved.
In the last two weeks the communist world has shown its point of view again on more than one occasion. Mr. Khrushchev has spoken in words that cannot be misunderstood regarding his relationships with Tito and with all communist nations that believe that communism can be a matter of nationalistic concern alone.
External Affairs
When my hon. friend mentions the needs of disarmament-and all of us in the free world hold that view-and of the hopes that he has that out of the conference in Geneva will come a measure of agreement that will permit of disarmament, I can only bring to his attention the fact that on the twelfth day of July Mr. Khrushchev said that the hope to work out a system of complete and fool-proof control over disarmament is unfounded. That is the atmosphere today in the communist world. 1 believe that the dynamism of the communist world will not be met by frozen negativism, and it is because I believe that that I took the stand in the House of Commons on Monday last when I set out something of the point of view of this government, something of our ideas and of our concepts of our responsibilities. The Secretary of State for External Affairs, the members of the government and myself agreed that whatever the purpose that Khrushchev may have had in mind in suggesting a summit meeting, for any of the nations of the free world, and in particular for the United Kingdom or the United States, to turn down that invitation preemptorily and without the fullest consideration of its import, the realization that it might convey a new hope for mankind, would be acting in a way detrimental to world peace.
I am very pleased this evening, as I have been throughout this day, as I have listened to the hon. members on the other side of the house join in their words of commendation of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, for after all, just as the Leader of the Opposition at one time occupied that position and at another time the former prime minister, Mr. St. Laurent-and generally through those days we in the opposition endeavoured to join as Canadians to achieve a degree of unity in foreign affairs-so on this occasion members of the opposition in generous terms have followed that course which is representative of true democracy within our country.
The hon. member for Essex East stated that in everything he would not agree. I would not expect that because after all there are bound to be disagreements as to the means being adopted, while agreement as to the objective is being maintained. It is because of that fact that a few days ago I stated I would welcome this debate with a view to having the views of the members of this house expressed on a matter that far transcends party affiliations or political consequences.
The stand that we as the government of this country take on this question is one that we hope will command the support of Canadians as a whole. Certainly the members of

External Affairs
the opposition on this occasion in the contributions that they have made have shown that realization of the gravity of the occasion and the necessity for closed ranks. In other words, each of us realizes that the events of the next few weeks may indeed have a tremendous influence not only on the future of our country but on the welfare of mankind.
I am going to refer to one or two suggestions made by the Leader of the Opposition this afternoon. One of the things that he suggested was an international police force and, as he said, that is no recent inovation or suggestion. Indeed, as I listened to him my mind went back 350 years in the reading of history to when the concept of an international police force was first brought to the attention of mankind by Grotius. The hon. member for Essex East referred to the league of nations and its failure in 1939. I think it failed prior to that when, in spite of the need of the establishment of an international force being generally recognized, it failed to secure the necessary support for the setting up of such a force, that aside from the fact that the restriction of the membership by the actions of one or two nations made it almost impossible for the league of nations to be a success.
I remember on one occasion hearing the late John W. Dafoe say that the only way in which mankind can preserve peace will be through the instrumentality of an international organization having the power to command respect and obedience to its commands and its determinations. The Leader of the Opposition has suggested that the general assembly might take steps towards the establishment of such a force. Under the uniting for peace resolution the general assembly has recognized the need for the existence of an armed force which could be used collectively notwithstanding the failure of the security council to discharge its responsibility. Article 43, to which reference was made by the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Essex East, is as follows:
1.	All members of the United Nations, in order to contribute to the maintenance of international peace and security, undertake to make available to the security council, on its call and in accordance with a special agreement or agreements, armed forces, assistance and facilities, including rights of passage, necessary for the purpose of maintaining international peace and security.
2.	Such agreement or agreements shall govern the numbers and types of forces, their degree of readiness and general location, and the nature of the facilities and assistance to be provided.
3.	The agreement or agreements shall be negotiated as soon as possible on the initiative of the security council. They shall be concluded between the security council and members or

between the security council and groups of members and shall be subject to ratification by the signatory states in accordance with their respective constitutional processes.
As the Leader of the Opposition said this afternoon, that has been the aim and purpose of successive meetings of the assembly but the achievement of that aim and ideal is still far removed. The general assembly has indeed recommended that states members maintain national armed forces elements for service as a United Nations unit or units upon recommendation by the security council or the general assembly.
Similar considerations which led to the enactment of the united for peace resolution or a development of the recommendations in that resolution might indeed lead to the establishment of some kind of permanent United Nations force, but there are, as was recognized here this morning, this afternoon and this evening, immense practical and political difficulties before agreement between the nations can be achieved. I am not going to give quotations this evening of some of the stands over the years in that behalf that have been taken by various members in the house. Suffice it to say that in March of 1945, prior to the convening of the United Nations conference in San Francisco, in common with other members of the house I advocated the need of the establishment of such a force. Later on in 1946 in the United Nations assembly Mr. St. Laurent advanced the proposition as one worthy of support.
But unfortunately as we look back on the perspective of events those who were in a position to bring about the achievement of that desirable end, without which peace under an international organization is founded on a slender reed, have made no great advance towards the attainment of this objective.
The Leader of the Opposition mentioned disarmament. I am going to refer to that a little later. He also dealt with the economic phase, as did the hon. member for Essex East, the need of assistance being given to underdeveloped countries. In that regard there are no boundaries to the attitude taken in support of that proposition by members in all parts of the house, and in the last year or so there have been material increases but that of itself is not sufficient.
One of the most serious challenges today is the challenge of the U.S.S.R. in its economic warfare, and in 1955 Khrushchev said, "We value trade least for economic reasons and most for political purposes." Everywhere in the world today the U.S.S.R. and the communist world generally are expanding their

trade relations without regard to profit considerations and Russia is measuring its success on the basis of the degree to which it is able to achieve control of the minds of those who for the moment trade economic advantage and ultimately lose their freedom. Only recently the New York Times made a survey of the trade offensive of the communist world and indicated that in 1955 communist trade exceeded $6 billion, that the communists have achieved footholds in 19 countries and that the increase in trade is double that of five years earlier. Indeed, at this very moment China is engaged in a trade offensive in Asia and Europe involving farm products, cement, textiles, manufactured products and the like. It affects us here. The U.S.S.R. is engaged in similar conduct with respect to aluminum, rails and general production.
I place before the house as worthy of attention that one of the courses we must take is the reconsideration of the resources of the international monetary fund and the international bank to the end that we will be able to achieve that degree of economic stability within the free world which will permit, indeed encourage the expansion of trade so that we can meet this offensive. For as the Leader of the Opposition said this afternoon, this is one of the major means being used by the communists today to undermine the stability and strength of the free world. The Secretary of State for External Affairs pointed out in a similar statement that the economic stage is one of the most important today, and one that challenges the free world by the tremendous danger that faces our trade and economic welfare by reason of this communist campaign.
I suggest that the international monetary fund, having played a useful part particularly in the last two or three years in helping countries tide over the rough spots in any balance of payments by making available short term loans in foreign exchange, mainly United States dollars, Canadian dollars and deutschemarks, deserves further assistance at this time. The fund has resources in gold-based currencies amounting to about $2,750 million, more than half of which are already committed in stand-by credits. I believe that consideration must be given to an increase in quotas of 50 per cent which would bring in an additional $3,000 million in gold and useful currencies, the result of which would be, according to the economists, substantially to increase the liquid assets underpinning world trade and give confidence to members of the fund that help would be available in case of need, so that they would not have to impose fresh import restrictions to deal with a temporary balance of payments problem.
External Affairs
In so far as the international bank is concerned, that position is also one that deserves attention. All the uncommitted countries of the world today look to the international bank for help in their development programs. The bank has become the main source of dollar capital for this purpose, with loan commitments now approaching $4,000 million. The main source of funds for lending is now the sale by the bank of its debentures to private investors. These debentures can be sold readily on account of the guarantee provided by the United States, and by other financially strong countries, of 80 per cent of their capital subscriptions. I suggest that if the bank continues to lend at the current rate it will, within a couple of years, have to issue additional debentures, which would bring its obligations within sight of the amounts guaranteed by the United States and Canada. In other words, by an increase of the guarantee from 80 per cent to 160 per cent of national capital subscriptions, there would be an increase in the banks borrowing power by several billions of dollars. Such action at this time would assure the less developed countries of the possibility of further assistance and would build a bulwark against the communist advance in the uncommitted countries. This would shore up those countries economically and give them new hope to meet the economic challenge of the communist world.
I mention this because the Leader of the Opposition dealt at some length with the need for economic action in the Middle East. His plan was a United Nations plan, as I understood it, the contributions to which were to be made by all countries, including the U.S.S.R. While naturally any step in that direction would be welcome, I am sure that the experience of the hon. gentleman in the past does not lead him to look too hopefully on the attainment of the objective that he mentioned, however desirable it might be.
Those were two of the matters to which the hon. gentleman gave particular attention. I come now to the question of a summit meeting. I betray no confidence when I say that the Secretary of State for External Affairs did, in the last week or ten days, give the leadership to break the deadlock which seemed to result from the original letter from Mr. Khrushchev offering a summit meeting. The press of our country have been generous, and have been mindful of his contribution and of the action taken, which I am glad, in general terms, has received the support of the opposition. The fact that we believe there is a responsibility in Canada in the Middle East as a threat to the world, is indicated by certain courses that are about to be adopted.

External Affairs
At the present time we have an ambassador in Cairo who is accredited to Lebanon, with Lebanon being in charge of a charge d'affaires. We have an ambassador in Athens who is accredited to Israel, and a charge d'affaires in Tel Aviv. With the problem of the Middle East so much in our minds, and the need of having the closest relationship with those countries so that we may be assured that our views shall receive full consideration and also to strengthen our relations both politically and commercially and, as I said a moment ago, through our missions, to increase our knowledge and understanding of the area, and of our confidence in its future, we intend within the next few days to initiate negotiations with the governments of Israel, Lebanon and Iran, with a view to setting up full, permanent diplomatic missions in the capitals of these three countries. These countries represent to us the standard bearers of freedom in that section of the Middle East which, up to the present time, have not received the diplomatic representatives which they had been desirous of having and have been entitled to have.
Having mentioned that, I now want to say a word in regard to the general question of a summit meeting, and some of the ideas and views that were held by the government with respect to this meeting. I think in the last few days events have moved very quickly. Mr. Khrushchev, having first advocated the necessity for a summit conference outside of the United Nations, finally agreed that the summit conference might be called in connection with the United Nations. It is the United Nations aspect of the forthcoming meeting that I think deserves the most serious consideration at this time.
I want to give you something of the thinking of the government on this matter for this meeting may well constitute a precedent for similar meetings in the future. Generally speaking, Khrushchev's prompt acceptance of the suggestion that the discussions between the representatives of the great powers should take place before the security council, not at a separate meeting at Geneva or elsewhere, does underline the authority of the United Nations. It was my view that any attempt to deal with the subject of the Middle East, with which the United Nations was seized, outside of the security council at this time would derogate from the real authority of the United Nations.
I think generally speaking-and it has been evidenced here today-there is reasonably general agreement that the proper auspices for the holding of this meeting should be under the aegis of the United Nations. There, there are rules of procedure which provide

for the calling together of a special group of nations as has been suggested, and any additional nations upon which the security council agree. In the interests of continuing peace which, after all, is the supreme purpose to which this country is dedicated, we believe there is being offered an opportunity to strengthen the security council and the United Nations by demonstrating that the rules that already are in existence which govern its activities are effective to deal with present problems. To have a separate meeting of nations to deal with specific problems which the security council itself has been discussing would, I repeat, be nothing less than a declaration to the whole world that the security council is incapable of carrying out the duties and responsibilities for which it was created.
We took a lead in this regard because while from the point of view of population we are still one of the smaller nations, we believe -and I think the belief is held generally throughout the whole world as the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) said -that smaller nations must be recognized and their rights upheld in the United Nations and the assurance of their viewpoint being placed before the United Nations maintained. It is for this reason that we take the view that a formal council meeting to initiate the talks between the heads of government concerned, after the procedure has been determined by the security council regular membership, should be attended by the heads of government able to be present. For it is in the full security council that the heads of government of the major powers, in whom our destiny rests in such large measure, can best explain their policies and having done so obtain the moral support needed to carry them out in accordance with the rule of law as symbolized in the charter of the United Nations.
It may not be possible for all heads of government to attend the special security council meeting of which I am thinking but I hope as many as possible will attend. I believe that they should request the great powers to meet and after quiet and reasoned discussion-the four powers to meet in private -to report to the security council on the issues. To this end Canada is prepared to take all necessary steps. Instructions are therefore going forward to our permanent representative to the United Nations to consult immediately with the secretary general, and with other delegations to the end that urgent consideration be given to the further steps necessary if this heads of government meeting of the security council is to pave the way for practical discussions and hoped for solutions of the problem which beset the

Middle East area. To that end we believe that some preparatory meetings of the security council, as I said a moment ago, in regular session will have to be held within the next few days to work out the details, for all of us must appreciate the fact that a top level meeting of that body, to the success of which mankind attaches such great importance, may take some little time to arrange.
In achieving this purpose and laying the proper foundation, we will be guided by the wisdom and experience of the secretary general in setting the necessary procedures in motion and a broad pattern will be sought. The procedure is something as follows. It will be first necessary to inscribe on the agenda of the security council in regular session an item sufficiently broad to permit not only a discussion of the problems of Lebanon and Jordan, of which the council is already seized, but to move on to those more deep-rooted issues which affect the area as a whole and of which, as the Leader of the Opposition said this afternoon, the Lebanese and Jordanian crises are but a manifestation.
When my hon. friend spoke this afternoon of the rise of Arab nationalism I thought of the book by Nasser entitled "Egypt's Liberation". That little book of 120 pages or so is the blueprint upon which Nasser has proceeded. He set the course out as clearly as ever did Hitler whose viewpoint in Mein Kampf few regarded seriously until it was too late. Indeed as one reads this book and sees something of the psychological influences which were referred to by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) this evening he realizes something of the tremendous forcefulness and tenacity of purpose which Nasser has exhibited in bringing about first among the peoples in that area a realization of their nationalism and also using that nationalism under the activating influence of the U.S.S.R. for purposes which brought about the conditions existing today in that area. After dreaming his dreams, giving his viewpoint, revealing his innermost thoughts, he says:
The pages of history are full of heroes who created for themselves roles of glorious valour which they played at decisive moments. Likewise the pages of history are full of heroic and glorious roles which never found heroes to perform them. For some reason it seems to me that within the Arab circle-
This book was written or published in 1955.
-there is a role, wandering aimlessly in search of a hero. And I do not know why it seems to me that this role, exhausted by its wanderings, has at last settled down, tired and weary, near the borders of our country and is beckoning to us to move, to take up its lines, to put on its costume, since no one else is qualified to play it.
External Affairs
There is the story. He took the role. He did what the Leader of the Opposition said today. He fomented. He aroused. He inspired. That is why, because of this matter of nationalism, the Arab countries cannot be taken for granted. It is one of the questions that deserves the most serious consideration by this summit meeting.
As far as the inscription is concerned, perhaps the item need be no more specific than "The Question of the Middle East", and I would hope that all members of the security council would find it possible thus to set the stage for discussions of an area which has been the focal point of so much strife and international tension in recent years. The heads of government when they meet at the special session of the security council, as I hope they will-and everything I have said is based on that meeting taking place- would address themselves to this broad problem and would express their concern and make available their ideas to those nations both in and out of the council whose interest in the Middle East is of a more direct nature. All of us recognize the primary responsibility of a few in this matter but the manner in which they discharge that responsibility is of vital concern to all nations great and small, both inside and outside the area concerned. Canada as a middle power occupying a strategic position wants the right to speak on this occasion.
As far as Canada is concerned, we believe that after the general discussion and after the opening statements, if that viewpoint is accepted in the security council, those principally concerned with the Middle East, namely the four or five powers mentioned by the Leader of the Opposition would be able to carry on their deliberations in private. I could not be more in agreement with the member for Essex East with respect to his remarks when he described what a conference of this kind might be if it were conducted under the glare of klieg lights and transmitted to all parts of the world by television. I believe we must free those at this meeting from the temptation to use it in order to turn it into a propaganda agency, for to do so would indeed be to hold back the advance of what I hope will be a reasonable degree of security in the Middle East and a realization, through discussion of the problems, by all parties, of the need for a decision to be arrived at.
If this were generally agreed Canada would be prepared to introduce a resolution at the special session of the security council calling on the permanent members most directly concerned with the Middle East to meet at the heads of government level in order to

External Affairs
carry forward the discussions initiated, in the council in full session, with the secretary general present in an appropriate capacity.
Some reference was made to the need for other nations to be called in, in particular India, and I am one of those who believe, with the Secretary of State for External Affairs that Mr. Nehru has a contribution to make at this time. Provision has already been made by article 31 of the charter which provides as follows:
Any member of the United Nations which is not a member of the security council may participate, without vote, in the discussion of any question brought before the security council whenever the latter considers that the interests of that member are specially affected.
Finally I would suggest that our resolution should call upon the secretary general to report the results of the private deliberations to the end that the people in the various countries concerned would have some knowledge of the discussions taking place. The question arises as to where to hold the meeting and much has been said about New York being the United Nations headquarters. Others have pointed out the possible dangers of holding a meeting in that city but there is naturally preference for New York out of regard for the necessity of preserving and consecrating, if I may use that word, the United Nations aspect of the proceedings which is of paramount importance. It would therefore seem logical on the whole to hold the initial high level security council meeting in New York but, if as a result of the general discussions or the full consideration of the problem in all its ramifications, it was decided that the meeting should be held elsewhere, I would remind the house that when I wrote to the Soviet union leader on January 18, 1958, I said:
You may be aware that there has been a suggestion in the Canadian House of Commons that the government might invite the participants in such a meeting to consider holding it in Canada. This suggestion was undoubtedly prompted by the consideration that Canada is the next-door neighbour of the United States and the U.S.S.R. and has a special relationship to commonwealth countries and to France. I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that when the participants decide that they are ready to call such a meeting and should they decide to hold it in Canada, they will be welcome.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
There are several other matters with which I wanted to deal on this occasion, including the matter of disarmament, but I think I have covered in general the immediate problem, namely that of the meeting and the attitude of Canada
towards that meeting. I repeat what I said originally that I believe Canadians as a whole are proud of the fact that Canada took the initiative in bringing about the attainment of this meeting in which the hopes of mankind will indeed be reposed.
In conclusion, I remember well, in April of 1945, at the United Nations meeting in San Francisco, seeing the beginnings of that organization and feeling the hopes then held for the success of a world organization which would preserve and maintain peace. The United Nations Organization has had its ups and downs since 1945. It now has what I believe is its appointment with destiny and I hope-and I am sure this hope is being expressed throughout the world not only in the free world but behind the iron curtain- that if the summit conference takes place, in good sense and with appreciation of the awful consequences of failure, the participants, through the security council, will go forward with the feeling that whatever the cost we must endeavour to attain at least some degree of assurance of security which has not existed in recent years. It is almost too much to hope for, but while there are some who say "why discuss these matters when past discussions have not been successful," I would like to remind the house that it has also been said, "While they are talking they are not fighting." One has only to go back to the remarks of Lord Grey in his memoirs when in reference to 1914 he said that if the nations in Europe had continued to talk rather than arriving at the conclusion that further talks were useless, world war I could and would have been prevented.
This meeting can be the crossroads for a new future. That is my hope and that hope has been shown in abundant measure today in the opening speech of the Secretary of State for External Affairs and in the contributions made by the Leader of the Opposition and the other hon. members who have spoken here.
Motion agreed to.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS NEWFOUNDLAND  TABLING OF REPORT OF ROYAL COMMISSION ON REVISION OF TERMS OF UNION

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS NEWFOUNDLAND  TABLING OF REPORT OF ROYAL COMMISSION ON REVISION OF TERMS OF UNION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to table, in English and in French, the report of the royal commission on Newfoundland finances. I wish to say that in the union of two states there are always many factors that require settlement and many divergent views have to be reconciled. Members of this house will recall the prolonged negotiations leading up to Newfoundland becoming a province of Canada on March 31, 1949.
It is not surprising that agreement was not readily reached. Although every effort was made to provide definitive terms for the entry of Newfoundland into the federation of Canada, it was found necessary to introduce a saving clause among the financial conditions. It was with respect to this reserve or saving clause, paragraph 29 of the terms of union, that the royal commission was concerned. The requirement that the financial results of union be examined within eight years by a federal royal commission was unique in the constitutional history of Canada. It is true that extensive studies have been conducted from time to time and adjustments made, in some cases, but in no other instance has there been a mandatory clause. The mandatory clause read as follows: The commission required to be appointed was-
-to review the financial position of the province of Newfoundland and to recommend the form and scale of additional financial assistance, if any, that may be required by the province of Newfoundland to enable it to continue public services at the levels and standards reached subsequent to the date of union, without resorting to taxation more burdensome, having regard to capacity to pay, than that obtaining generally in the region comprising the maritime provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Prince Edward Island.
After full consideration of the terms of reference, the commissioners have concluded that the burden of taxation in the province of Newfoundland does not differ materially from that in the maritime provinces. It is their opinion, after studying the course of provincial finances since union, that additional financial assistance is necessary if the province is to maintain the levels and standards of public services reached.
Accordingly, basing their recommendations on the anticipated results of the fiscal year 1957-58, they have recommended that an annual payment be made to the province of $8 million a year, commencing on April 1, 1957, this amount to be reduced by the amount of any transitional grant that may still be payable.
The government will study the report and its recommendations and will decide upon the appropriate course of action. The decision will thus bring finality to the terms of union of Newfoundland and Canada.
The government is most grateful to the commissioners for their efforts in meeting the obligation in the terms of union.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF AGREEMENT COVERING CONSTRUCTION OF DAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like now to make an announcement in regard to the South Saskatchewan river dam project agreement. The agreement was signed this morning by the Minister of Agriculture, having previously been signed by Premier Douglas on behalf of the province of Saskatchewan.
The signing of this agreement with the province of Saskatchewan represents an important step forward in the development of Canada's resources. Its main objective is, through its large-scale water conservation
2854	HOUSE OF
Irrigation-South Saskatchewan River and irrigation potentialities, to provide stability for agriculture in central Saskatchewan, where droughts, sometimes prolonged, have in the past created serious problems for more than 50,000 farmers, a truth that is driven home by conditions this season.
While many think of irrigation as associated particularly with the production of specialty crops, it may be that the production under irrigation of alfalfa and other fodder crops in the centre of Saskatchewan's most populous farming area and in quantities sufficient to remove the fear of having to sacrifice livestock because of feed shortages in drought years or having to bring in fodder from other areas at great expense will prove to be the greatest benefit in the long run.
I say the greatest benefit. But irrigation possibilities represent by no means the only good to flow from the project that the signing of this agreement will inaugurate. The construction of the earth dam now agreed upon will make possible the production of hydroelectric power on a scale that will mean much to the industrial development of the province, while the assurance of adequate water supplies for such cities as Regina and Moose Jaw and the control of flooding are benefits that in the minds of many would of themselves justify much of the outlay that will be called for in carrying out this vast project.
It has been under discussion for many years. The need has been there, and it has been very obvious. I look back a matter of 25 years to the time when the question was first given consideration and discussion. Again after 1940 when I represented Lake Centre constituency, as it then was, within which a portion of the dam will be located, discussions continued. Fifteen years ago investigations were begun by P.F.R.A. officials, and during the past decade these investigations have been continued to determine the feasibility and economic importance of the project. Naturally I am happy that the project is now inaugurated, and I am sure the country as a whole will share my satisfaction.
I have stressed the irrigation possibilities, possibilities that may one day see water brought to 500,000 acres of Saskatchewan's good lands, the immense power development potentialities and the assurance of water supplies. There are many other benefits that will accrue as a result of the building of the dam. The control of water levels in the Qu'Appelle valley and its lakes, as well as the formation of a completely new great lake of the South Saskatchewan river system upstream from the dam, will provide recreational facilities and wildlife possibilities that will doubtless be appreciated by generations to come, and


may well become one of the major tourist attractions in the western provinces.
I am very happy that this project is now in a position where construction can proceed, and I am sure members in all parts of the house will hope that out of the completion of this project will come for agriculture within that area of Saskatchewan and for Saskatchewan and the western provinces generally the dawning of a new day.

speakeroldname: Hon. Sidney E. Smith (Secretary of Slate for External Affairs) moved:
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That items numbered 85 to 111, inclusive, item numbered 502, items numbered 542 to 549, inclusive, and item numbered 655, as listed in the main and supplementary estimates 1958-59, relating to the Department of External Affairs be withdrawn from the committee of supply and referred to the standing committee on external affairs, saving always the powers of the committee of supply in relation to the voting of public moneys.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in speaking to this motion I must confess that I have at the present time a feeling of anxiety with respect to international affairs, yet I hasten to add that that anxiety is brightened by a sense of hope, hope which is not founded on wishful thinking.
I am sure members will be happy to hear that I do not intend this morning to give the house a global survey of the international situation as it affects Canada, either directly or indirectly. Rather, I propose to deal with certain factors which very closely concern us at this time.
The first item, of course, with which the house will expect me to deal is the grave and vital situation in the Middle East. I am sure there is no need for me to rehearse in detail the developments in that area during the past two weeks, because members are no doubt familiar with those developments; but with respect to Canada, and indeed the whole world, our attention is directed to New York, and I propose at the beginning of my remarks to give to the house a full account of the latest happenings there.
Before doing so, however, I should make reference to the developments in Lebanon leading up to this particular crisis, and give to the house some information with respect to the evolution of that crisis. Members will recall that on May 27, 1958, Lebanon presented charges to the security council of the United Nations simultaneously with those to the Arab league. The charge of Lebanon was that the United Arab Republic had intervened in its internal affairs. The Arab league had nothing to offer in the way of a solution of the issues involved in this charge and subsequently the security council, after discussion of the charges, decided to act in this particular regard.
May I remind the house, however, that there had never been any overt aggression from Syria into Lebanon. It had to do with indirect aggression. This was a new type of aggression with which the security council had to deal. It is difficult to define what

is indirect aggression, yet the security council addressed itself to this question.
I may interpolate here that for some time the United Nations has been endeavouring without success to define indirect aggression, and certainly it was understood and recognized that the security council had power to investigate charges with respect to that type of intervention, indirect though it be, in the affairs of another country. And so on June 11 the security council set up an observation group, and I read part of the text of the resolution:
-to ensure that there is no illegal infiltration of personnel or supply of arms or other materiel across the Lebanese borders.
The government of Canada considered that the situation which was unfolding in Lebanon merited prompt action. From the beginning in the discussions in the security council we gave our firm support to this resolution, a resolution that provided machinery under the auspices of the United Nations. We welcomed the resolution, Mr. Speaker, by reason of the fact that it afforded to the secretary general an opportunity to contribute to the stabilization of the situation in Lebanon. We also welcomed the ambit of the resolution that gave certain flexibility to the secretary general in carrying out or implementing the resolution's objectives.
That resolution was adopted on June 11. There was no veto and no dissenting vote. On that particular occasion, and it was very encouraging, the U.S.S.R. abstained from voting on the resolution. The secretary general then moved very quickly, and within a few days he had officers of his observation corps present in Lebanon. Hon. members will recall that Canada immediately responded to the appeal from the secretary general and sent ten officers to join the observation group. Indeed, Canada at the moment has 11 officers there. A Canadian officer who was attached to the United Nations truce supervision organization was seconded to the observation group in Lebanon.
This group, the United Nations observation group in Lebanon, has become known as UNOGIL, and that is the designation I shall use. It encountered at the outset many difficulties in carrying out its task. Initially the group had access to only 18 kilometers out of the 324 kilometers of Lebanon's frontier with Syria. Other difficulties were encountered by reason of the rugged nature of the terrain, the location of the border populations, and also by reason of the traditional freedom of people to move across the border from Syria to Lebanon, a freedom they have had for many years. Here was a fairly
57071-3-168
External Affairs
recent boundary line between Syria and Lebanon. Many of these initial difficulties, however, were overcome by the middle of July and the observer group, UNOGIL, had access to all the frontier areas between Lebanon and Syria. They had been increased in numbers and personnel and were also getting aircraft for the purpose of carrying out their directives from the secretary general.
During recent weeks there has been one frontier of Lebanon that has been quiet. That is the frontier with Israel. Indeed, I would point out that during this difficult period all of Israel's frontiers have been quiet. That is a tribute to Israel, to the United Arab Republic and to other countries, and it is also a tribute to the effectiveness of two other United Nations organizations, the United Nations emergency force along the Egyptian-Israeli armistice line and the United Nations truce supervision organization on Israel's other frontier.
Now to return to the narrative of events that I anticipated a few moments ago I would give. On July 14 there occurred the sudden, swift and violent revolution in Iraq which transformed the situation in the Middle East overnight. Within Lebanon it appeared still further to exacerbate internal dissensions and-of this I am convinced-the happenings in Iraq rendered UNOGIL incapable, at least temporarily, of meeting its responsibilities, in the dangerous situation thus created. And so it was in this situation that President Eisenhower responded promptly and affirmatively to a request from President Chamoun of Lebanon. As President Eisenhower stated at the time of the landing of United States troops in Lebanon, the force was not there to engage in hostilities but to help Lebanon in its own efforts to stabilize the situation until-and I emphasize that word "until"-the United Nations could take the steps necessary to protect Lebanon's independence and integrity.
Two days later, as we recall, the United Kingdom found it necessary to take similar emergency action in response to an appeal from King Hussein of Jordan for military assistance in the face of a plot instigated from outside Jordan to overthrow the regime. I have been informed reliably, and I know, that there was not only a plot to overthrow the government in Jordan but also that the plot extended to other countries in the Middle East to overthrow their governments.
As the Prime Minister informed the house on July 17, the Canadian government appreciated that the United States and the United Kingdom had no alternative but to take these interim measures. We knew then that both governments had stated specifically that the

External Affairs
landing of troops and the keeping of troops there would be terminated as soon as the United Nations could take effective action. We understood the difficulty of the decision that the two countries, the United Kingdom and the United States, had been forced to take.
To return to the point I attempted to make a moment ago, we recognized clearly that the United Kingdom and the United States appreciated the ultimate authority and responsibility of the United Nations.
Since that time we in Canada have made every effort at the United Nations and in some of the capitals of the world to bring about as swiftly as possible those United Nations actions which would provide some instrumentality of the United Nations to the end that the United States would withdraw their forces from Lebanon and the United Kingdom would withdraw their forces from Jordan.
In the United Nations security council, the United States and the United Kingdom have joined, or we have joined with them and other countries, in promoting steps that would provide personnel on behalf of and under the United Nations that would in turn enable those two countries to withdraw their forces. To this end we gave full support last week to a draft resolution submitted to the security council by the United States. In brief, the purpose of that resolution was to enable the secretary general to establish an instrumentality-and the type of instrument would be in his good judgment-that would add to the forces of UNOGIL now in Lebanon. We supported that; yet at the end of last Friday, just one week ago, the Russians vetoed that proposal. That was on July 18.
With respect to my own activities at this time, I may say that I had flown to Washington where I had valuable discussions with Mr. Dulles and Mr. Selwyn Lloyd, a valuable exchange of views. The newspapers have quoted me as taking the stand on behalf of Canada that there should be no expansion of military activities by these two countries, that is, outside of Lebanon and Jordan. The Prime Minister has also taken that stand, and he has so informed the house. From Washington I went to New York, where I had discussions with Mr. Hammarskjold. Then I came here to report fully on the situation as I saw it to the Prime Minister.
I got off the aeroplane on Saturday and heard for the first time that Mr. Khrushchev had extended an invitation for a summit meeting on the Middle East. At the Prime Minister's request I went back to New York on Monday morning where I took charge of the

Canadian delegation, and I seized the opportunity then to express the hope that nations would respond to the invitation issued by Mr. Khrushchev for a summit meeting on the Middle East. I shall deal with that matter later.
On that particular day the Prime Minister informed the house that on Monday morning he had sent messages to Mr. Eisenhower, Mr. Macmillan, Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, and Mr. Nehru, and in those messages he expressed the hope that there would not be a negative reaction to the proposal put forward by Mr. Khrushchev.
In New York on Monday and Tuesday of last week our delegation worked very closely with the delegations from the United Kingdom, the United States and Japan in an endeavour to work out a compromise resolution which might be more acceptable to the Russians than the one they vetoed on Friday last, which had been put forward by the United States. This particular resolution was put forward by the Japanese. We were rather hopeful of this resolution that provided in its operative part for an increase in the observer group of UNOGIL and gave further authority to the secretary general to endeavour to stabilize the situation in Lebanon to the end that the United States could withdraw its forces.
As I said in the meeting of the security council on Monday of last week in support of this resolution, I deemed it a positive approach, one which offered the council an opportunity to use and strengthen the United Nations machinery that it had in Lebanon; but this, too, the Soviet union vetoed. And so, as far as the activities of the United Nations in Lebanon are concerned, we are back where we were at the beginning of last week. However, after the veto the secretary general expressed his determination to use the powers that had been voted to him on June 11 by the security council, and he said he would firmly proceed to implement his mandate in the resolution of the date to which I referred. I think it would be of interest to the house if I read a part of the statement the secretary general made on Tuesday afternoon after the veto of the Japanese resolution by the U.S.S.R. Mr. Hammarskjold said:
I am sure that I will act in accordance with the wishes of the members of the council if I therefore use all opportunities offered to the secretary general within the limits set by the charter toward developing the United Nations effort so as to help to prevent a further deterioration of the situation in the Middle East, and to assist in finding a road away from the dangerous point at which we now find purselves.
Even before the Japanese resolution failed of adoption Mr. Hammarskjold had decided

to increase the personnel of the UNOGIL in Lebanon from about 135 officers to something approximating 200, and he requested Canada to send three additional observers. The Prime Minister has informed the house of Canada's ready response to that invitation from Mr. Hammarskjold, and I recall the words the Prime Minister uttered in this house, that Canada was willing to take that action, ready to do it, glad to do it, and then he made this statement:
Canada will supply immediately three of the additional observers, of course giving every attention to any further requirement of UNOGIL as events transpire.
Therefore what is needed now is an expansion, of the scope and importance of UNOGIL activity. The hon. member for Essex East asked a question on Wednesday of this week. I was not in the house at the time. The hon. member asked whether Canada had received any further invitation from the secretary general for additional personnel from this country. No invitation has come forward as yet, but Mr. Hammarskjold intimated on Tuesday afternoon at the meeting of the security council that if the Russians vetoed the Japanese resolution he would go to work immediately and evolve a plan for the increase in that particular group. That plan is now, we know, being developed but it has not yet been made final.
Members of the house may recall, Mr. Speaker, that at the time of the establishment of UNEF Mr. Hammarskjold, the secretary general of the United Nations, associated with himself an advisory committee of member states to assist him in the conduct of his task with respect to UNEF. There are indications now that Mr. Hammarskjold will invite certain countries to send representatives to such an advisory committee, and it may well be that he will choose the personnel of the advisory committee of UNEF, the advisory committee that has been in being for some time.
So that is where we stand now. A new United Nations body, not new since Tuesday afternoon but new since June 11, has been developed and set up, and we hope this body will be effective in enabling the Lebanese people to work out their own internal difficulties and dissensions in their own way. I have confidence that such a United Nations body, developed under a plan still to be presented by the secretary general, will be effective in establishing stability.
But what of the future? Is there a way to ensure permanently the independence and integrity of this small country with its unique balance of east and west, with its unique composition of population, about half Arab, 57071-3-168i
External Affairs
half Moslem and half Christian? There were discussions in Washington while I was there-
