speechtext:
I am sorry for that slip. The information I have is that it was roughly fifty-fifty as between Moslems and Christians. The Moslem group, incidentally, is broken up into two parts, one part Levantine and the other part Arab. I will seek to verify my information and if I am wrong I will tell the hon. member. We had discussions in Washington about the future of Lebanon. The discussions had to do with the possibility of having the Lebanese accept a position of neutrality. Favour was expressed by the United States and United Kingdom representatives with respect to that proposal.
I was not here on Monday, but I have read the address of that distinguished representative of a member of the commonwealth, the Prime Minister of Ghana. I know that he also advanced that proposal when he addressed members of the house in joint session with members of the Senate. Can we work toward a status of neutrality for Lebanon and have an international guarantee of its neutrality such as is provided in effect for Austria? It cannot be imposed on the Lebanese, but it should not come as a novel suggestion to them because throughout the centuries, indeed from Phoenician times, the Lebanese have been merchants and traders. Their history shows that by reason of necessity to be friendly with as many people as possible in order to trade with them, they have over the centuries achieved that relationship with bordering countries.
Of course there is a new factor, one that I adverted to earlier in my remarks. Recently Lebanon has been rocked by pressures, sometimes violent pressures, from outside countries. Recently those pressures have been manifested in hostile radio broadcasts and other activities, and these pressures have brought about the vexed situation in which the Lebanese find themselves at this particular time. But it is, I think, possible to find a way out of the situation along the lines I suggested a moment ago. I would expect that the Lebanese might welcome some arrangement establishing neutrality that would assure them their independence in this middle position. But I am convinced that that cannot be brought about without the practical assistance of the United Nations. Indeed, I think it might well require some physical manifestation of United Nations authority, a physical manifestation of such authority on the ground in Lebanon.

External Affairs
The task which the observer group is now performing and will perform to a greater and more successful degree, I hope, will be to insulate the political affairs of Lebanon from those of its neighbours and thus help to restore tranquility in that divided nation. That, Mr. Speaker, could be the forerunner of some continuing role on the part of the United Nations in that country, perhaps not unlike the role played not by the United Nations but by Canada and other members of the international commissions in Indochina. As hon. members will recall, these commissions were set up by the Geneva agreements of 1954.
In putting forward this suggestion I realize that the United Nations should proceed cautiously, but if the experiment were successful it might be used as a precedent for stabilizing other countries in the Middle East, torn not only by fierce internal antagonisms but by hostile external rivalries and tensions. The possibility of insulation through the United Nations raises novel problems and vast difficulties, but so acute have the problems of this region become that we must cast our minds about to examine every possible line of approach which might offer the prospect of advance.
I make another reference to the stability not only of Lebanon but also of the Middle East. Much of their trouble can be traced to the economic difficulties in which they find themselves, and I would hope it would be possible to give some assurance of economic stability not only to Lebanon but to the whole Middle East that would warrant and promote political stability. In this particular task I can foresee for the United Nations and for other organizations a really valuable role.
As the Prime Minister said the other day in the house, this is not the time for stagnant thinking, and if there is anything in this new United Nations approach, the west could seize the opportunity at the summit meeting which now appears certain to be held in New York and endeavour to make a small beginning, at any rate, in the country of Lebanon.
That was one reason that prompted the Canadian government to welcome the Soviet proposal of last Saturday, a proposal that contained offensive and provocative language giving unnecessary offence to the addressees. Indeed, I had occasion to point out to Mr. Sobolev when I was in New York that it was unnecessarily truculent and offensive. But I know I can speak for the Prime Minister when I say that in sending messages to President Eisenhower, Mr. Macmillan and Mr. Nehru, expressing hope that there would

not be a negative attitude to Mr. Khrushchev's proposal, we had in mind that some constructive measure such as the one I have been indicating might be looked at and adopted not only for Lebanon but for the Middle East.
Then with reference to the message that was received by France, the United Kingdom and the United States from Mr. Khrushchev, we had in mind that a meeting at the top could result in a diminution of international tension. On Sunday we discussed also the terrible possibility, not the probability but the terrible possibility, of the nations of the world sliding into a global nuclear war. The leaders of the governments of this generation would never be forgiven if they did not exhaust every possible way of relieving, at least in some measure, international tension.
This was another basis for the messages that went out from the Prime Minister over the week end. I can claim that in this regard Canada took the lead. The public expression of the desire of this government to promote the holding of a summit meeting was the first public utterance on the western side in this respect. I took the opportunity in the security council, as did the Prime Minister when he informed the house on Monday, of making very clear our concept of the desirability of holding an international conference as suggested. I have in mind, but I cannot claim this, that my observations had something to do with the postponement at least of the U.S.S.R. proposal to call for a general assembly meeting in which they could indulge in more propaganda.
I have in mind also that the stand of the Canadian government, as expressed by me in the security council on Monday of last week, had something to do with the acceptance of the counterproposal put forward by Mr. Macmillan on behalf of the United Kingdom. The real significance to me of the resolution with respect to the holding of a meeting in the security council-I do now expect it will be a favourable decision-is that this meeting will be held under the aegis of the United Nations. The security council, and I quote from the United Nations charter, was established for the following purpose:
In order to ensure prompt and effective action by the United Nations, its members confer on the security council primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security, and agree that in carrying out its duties under this responsibility the security council acts on their behalf.
In my opinion, that is the proper forum for a meeting of Mr. Macmillan, Mr. Khrushchev, Mr. Eisenhower, General de Gaulle and others.

We have noted with encouragement that Mr. Khrushchev has responded to this proposal that was sent out in clearer terms, perhaps, from London than from any other capital, that this meeting should be held within the security council. It could be, it may be- I emphasize the word "may"-a meeting of momentous consequence. Again, I say that it is worth trying in terms of the voice of humanity. Furthermore, I have in mind that apart from the powers whom I have named and to whom the letters were addressed by the author, the presence of Mr. Nehru, the distinguished leader of one of the nations of the commonwealth and a representative of the awakening world of Asia, would contribute much to such a conference.
With reference to the eventual composition of the conference, I am sure that the house will have noted the observations made yesterday by Right Hon. Mr. Macmillan at Westminster. These are his words:
I am glad to note Mr. Khrushchev's latest letter recognizes . . . (that) . . . until the form of the meeting has been agreed it would be premature to lay down which countries, which are not members of the security council, should attend, or by whom they should be represented.
I agree with that particular view, at this stage, when there will have to be negotiations with respect to the time, with respect to the agenda and other matters. I would say this, however; that it will be for the security council to decide what nations, which are not members of the security council, should come to the table of the security council. That is a procedural matter for the security council. I saw it in operation on Monday and Tuesday of this week, for example. The council, by formal resolution presented by the chairman before one meeting on Monday started and before the two meetings on Tuesday started, asked the representatives of the United Arab Republic, Lebanon and Jordan to come and be present at the council table. I say again, Mr. Speaker, that is a matter fcrr the security council to decide.
However, I express anxiety lest these matters having to do with who will sit and who will go to the meeting should jeopardize the holding of that meeting. Questions of this sort should not be insuperable or prevent the proposed meeting of the security council. In my opinion they should be treated and considered as secondary. With respect to this meeting in New York, whatever the date may be, I have in mind that it is desirable also, if some means can be found, to have the opinions of the numerous countries concerned, because no plan that may be evolved in the security council will be successful
External Affairs
unless the proposals are accorded the approval of the peoples of those regions.
One of the problems we in Canada must always keep in mind is a concern, for example, lest the prosperity of Israel should not be safeguarded in the forthcoming negotiations. Surely it will be possible to get the views of the Middle East countries whatever the procedural device may be. Many problems, as I indicated a moment ago, will arise on the subject of time, on the subject of the agenda and prior consultation. But when the Prime Minister spoke in this house on July 25 about the possibility of holding such a meeting within the security council he deliberately used words which took into account the flexible procedure that would have to be devised if this conference is to be brought into being.
I would express on behalf of Canada the hope that we will have this concept of flexibility. It is here, I believe, that the secretary general, with his great experience and wisdom which he has shown particularly during the past two weeks, could be given the opportunity of devising some formula within the existing United Nations structure in order to enable these important conclusions to be reached with respect to those matters to which I referred, and to the end that the consultations at New York will be fruitful.
It is not inappropriate that I announce at this time an important development in connection with the responsibilities of Canada in Indo-China. I would just bring back to the attention of the members of the house the role that Canada has played through its membership in three international commissions in Indo-China; one international commission in Laos, one in Cambodia and one in Viet Nam. That was an example I used a few moments ago. Here were powers sitting down at Geneva in 1954 to deal with dissensions in these three parts of IndoChina. There was in that particular area the possibility, indeed the probability, of a collision of the communist powers on the one side and western countries on the other.
What was done? There was established at the Geneva meeting machinery whereby the situation in these three countries could be stabilized or helped to be stabilized through the presence of international commissions. Canada was and is a member of those international commissions in the three countries, the other members being India and Poland. With the physical manifestation, if nothing else, of these three international commissions the result was that in Laos the royal government was enabled to bring about the stabilization of the situation there.

External Affairs
There was a reconciliation oi the communist forces and the royal force and there came about stability. On May 4 of this year supplementary elections were held in Laos and they indicated to Canada that its task had been performed in Laos through its membership in that commission.
Hence I informed the house recently that the Canadian delegation to the international commission for supervision and control in Laos had introduced a resolution calling for the dissolution of the commission. I wish now to inform the house that the international commission for Laos was adjourned sine die on July 19. There were forces at work there -and you can guess their origin-which resisted the retirement or the adjournment of the Laos international commission.
In the end Canada joined with others in bringing about this adjournment sine die. We made it very clear that we were not getting out by reason of any threats or suggestions by Laotians, but we had in mind the representations made here by Souvanna Phouma, the Prime Minister of Laos, that after the election had been held and the situation stabilized, he felt that the commission would have performed its task. That commission can be reconvened in Laos at the call of the chairman, the representative for India. Canada must be consulted. If we go back by reason of any particular emergency we will always have in mind the rights of the Laotian government, and we will not interfere with the sovereignty of that country. In the opinion of the Canadian government the commission which began its operations in 1954 has completed its task.
With respect to Viet Nam there is tension, as the members of the house well know, between South and North Viet Nam. That situation has not been stabilized. There is a need for the continuation of the work of the international commission in Viet Nam, but we have advice that we can apply a formula similar to the Laos one to Cambodia where the situation has been stabilized.
I seize this opportunity to pay tribute to India, which provided a chairman, for its co-operation, and also to pay a tribute to the success of the royal government in Laos in bringing about a reconciliation of the two forces that were indeed hostile to one another. We will now take up the problem with respect to Cambodia. As I indicated a moment ago, we should be able to use the same formula of adjournment.
I come back to this concept that I advanced earlier with respect to Lebanon and with respect to certain other countries in the Middle East. Is there not something in the example of the success of the international

commissions in Laos and Cambodia for a solution of some of the problems at least in some of the trouble spots in the Middle East?
I will now speak on the problem of disarmament. It may be that some will have the thought that we should not be talking about disarmament in the particularly vexed situation that we now have. I do not share that view. Indeed, the interest in and the desire for disarmament have been intensified by events in the past few weeks. In order to provide members of the house a perspective with respect to disarmament, a perspective that will be read with deeper concern during the present situation, I am tabling a white paper with respect to the disarmament discussions in 1957.
I need hardly recall for the information of the house the breakdown of the negotiations that were carried on through the subcommittee of the commission on disarmament established by the United Nations. France, the United Kingdom, the United States and Canada put forward certain proposals on August 29 of last year. They appeared to be a package deal, if I can use that expression. Since the time negotiations broke down, the Russians having flatly rejected the proposals, the countries of the west including Canada have been endeavouring to make clear that those proposals of August 29, 1957, were merely put forward as a basis of discussion. Indeed the Prime Minister in the general assembly last year and I myself in the political committee of the United Nations and in the general assembly urged that the Russians look at those proposals as being flexible. But that situation was not accepted by the U.S.S.R., and little if anything has been done within the United Nations since last autumn with respect to disarmament.
However, there have been some encouraging signs recently of a resumption of negotiations. We were all gratified that President Eisenhower felt it possible to make a suggestion with respect to one kind of disarmament or with respect to certain measures that could lead to one kind of disarmament, and he put those forward to Mr. Khrushchev. We are gratified and encouraged to hear that Mr. Khrushchev has accepted the proposal to establish a technical group for the purpose of examining the possibility of providing adequate supervision and control of nuclear tests and methods for the detection of nuclear tests.
The discussions began in Geneva on July 1 of this year with respect to the scientific problems involved. Even if I knew what had been happening at those discussions I would not understand the scientific problems, but I can say it is authoritatively reported that

the talks between the scientists are making headway in an encouraging manner. Without attempting to predict the final outcome of this scientific conference, I am confident that significant findings will be made by this technical group. Canada, as the house knows, is represented there by Dr. O. M. Solandt who has associated with him four other Canadian scientists. The other Canadians are Mr. H. Larnder and Mr. A. K. Longair of the defence research board, Dr. P. L. Willmore of the dominion observatory and Professor G. M. Volkotf of the University of British Columbia.
The government has held the view that after the findings of this group are made known, in which findings we feel confidence could be placed, a method might be arrived at by which to detect nuclear tests, and then the countries carrying on such tests might come to a political agreement with respect to the cessation of these tests. This is a view which has been advanced by the Prime Minister throughout the country on several occasions; but let me say that the detection and inspection, the control and supervision of nuclear tests do not constitute in themselves a measure of disarmament. They are a means to ensure disarmament; they provide sanctions for a political agreement with respect to a type of disarmament, and I would express the hope that after the successful conclusion of the present technical studies there might be taken what could be regarded as a step having a revolutionary effect on the international climate.
An initial move might be made with respect to the cessation of further nuclear tests, and in that way there might be established some element of mutual trust and confidence, after which the nations concerned could move on to the more complex aspects of a disarmament program. The suspension of nuclear tests with these guarantees as to detection could constitute the first step toward agreement, which agreement would in turn be the first step toward disarmament, even though this would not be the most important measure, which is that having to do with the use of nuclear weapons already proved.
There is another encouraging factor on which I would like to report with respect to disarmament. Mr. Eisenhower proposed that it would be useful to study practical measures to provide required safeguards against surprise attacks and we have been heartened by a rather affirmative reply by Mr. Khrushchev. We in Canada should promote in every possible way the holding of a meeting of experts of a somewhat similar nature to the present Geneva meeting with respect to the detection of nuclear tests, in order to study means and methods of preventing surprise attacks. This is a matter which is, of course,
External Affairs
of very direct concern to this country with particular reference to surprise attacks over the Arctic region.
I am sure I need not spell out the implications of this matter or draw a picture of what we have advocated in this regard. I reported on our advocacy at the Copenhagen meeting. The Russians have indicated-and this I would like to emphasize-that they might be willing to sit down with such a group. I do not think a political agreement would be necessary at this stage, any more than it has been necessary to enter into a political agreement with respect to the holding of nuclear tests while the current meeting of scientists is being held. I propose, however, that experts should be brought together in order to study this further problem.
One cannot anticipate the measures which the experts would put forward. They may have to do with electronic or radar devices, or they may be along the lines of ground inspection as proposed by the U.S.S.R., which could operate rather simply as a bilateral exchange of inspectors, or a more strictly supervised international system might be involved under the control of the United Nations. We could, however, make progress in this regard.
The U.S.S.R. has on many occasions replied to the proposal for detection or knowledge of the possibility of surprise attack over the Arctic that this really does not matter very much. To us in Canada, however, it does matter, and the Prime Minister indicated last summer that for the operation of a scheme to prevent surprise attack all of the Canadian territory would be made available on a reciprocal basis if the Russians would give a similar undertaking.
The proposal has now been made by the United States and Canada that both countries would throw open their territories to inspection to ensure against surprise attacks if the Russians would do likewise, but the U.S.S.R. wants this system extended to the United States bases in Europe. The United States has said, we will throw open Europe from the Atlantic to the Urals, but if we go as far as Europe will you also agree to allow inspections of that kind? It seems to me, however, that without decisions at this time as to the exact location of such inspections we would at least make a start by arranging a meeting of experts to consider effective technical measures which could be taken in the event that such a political agreement were made.
To come back to the Arctic area, it would be easier to establish a system of control and supervision in that region than it would be in the more populous areas of the North American continent; but we must arrive at

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house will, I am sure, have listened with great interest and appreciation to the statement of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. He has covered many important subjects, more particularly perhaps one which is very much in our minds at the present time. If he will permit me to use the expression, in recent days he has been a winged mercury flying backward and forward from here to New York, to Washington, in the search with others for a solution to an international crisis which is centred in a part of the world which may seem to be very far from Canada but which in terms of its effect is very close to Canada. He has been seeking a solution which, if it can be found, will reduce tensions and strengthen security and which, if it cannot be found, will add to those tensions and diminish that security.
I know the minister must have had a very exhausting time in recent days. I know that his work has been not only exhausting but at times it must have been frustrating, but I know also he has found it rewarding and that he has received great satisfaction out of the opportunity he has been given. I know too that he has taken full advantage of that opportunity in making on behalf of the government a contribution to the search for international peace and security, which is a search in which we are all engaged in one form or another.
I can assure him and the government on behalf of the opposition that our good wishes go with them in the work he is doing, and we wish him well. He has covered some important subjects. There are some, of course, which he has not had the time to cover and this resolution before us now, which will permit the setting up of the committee on external affairs, will give us a chance in the committee to go into some of these matters which we have not the opportunity of discussing today.
There are many subjects and there is little time. I would like to begin by making a reference-and it will be only a brief reference; some of my colleagues may follow it up later-to the United Nations and its activities in recent weeks and months. It has shown itself once again to be an indispensable piece of international machinery even when it has

External Affairs
not been effective. We have once again had driven in upon us that when trouble starts and when the big powers do not want to get into it, or want to get out of it after they have got into it, they go to the United Nations and seek-and it is right, of course, that they should seek-ways out of their difficulty through our world organization.
The United Nations now, as in the past, is being asked-thank goodness it is being asked -to come to the rescue, to stop trouble spreading. But while that is a vital role to be playing, especially at this time, even more important is the role of the United Nations in preventing trouble. We sometimes forget -the minister reminded us of this aspect of its work today-that trouble-preventing role, that positive and constructive role of the United Nations in the humanitarian, social, economic and co-operation fields; but the core and centre of its responsibilities are its political activities in its efforts to prevent war. That, of course, is where we encounter at the United Nations and elsewhere our real difficulty.
Perhaps the best example of that difficulty has been given by the minister himself in his statement this morning, when he referred to the work in the United Nations and indeed of committees outside the United Nations on disarmament, the agonizing attempt which has been made now for so many years-and I recall when it began with the old League of Nations in the late 1920's-the efforts to reconcile security and disarmament and to decide which comes first.
I welcome the white paper which the minister has been good enough to table this morning and which will perhaps give us the basis for a useful discussion of this matter in the committee on external affairs.
We are getting toward the end of July. This reminds us that the United Nations annual assembly will soon be taking place. I have no doubt that the Canadian government are now beginning to discuss and decide what attitude they should adopt at this assembly. I would like, if I might, to mention three things in which I think it might be helpful if Canada could take the initiative. Indeed, I think in at least one matter Canada has already taken an initiative. That initiative might be followed up. The first matter is I think of great importance at the present time, an importance which should not be obscured by the immediate international crisis in the Middle East which occupies so much of our time and attention, if it can be done-and I do not know where it can be done except at the United Nations-is to try to halt the spread of the manufacture of nuclear weapons to other than the three countries which now do manufacture them.

I quite appreciate the difficulties in the way. For that purpose would it not be desirable to explore at the forthcoming United Nations assembly the possibility of a resolution which might get the necessary acceptance and which would embody a self-denying principle accepted by all the other members of the United Nations in regard to the prohibition in their own territory of the manufacture of any atomic weapon of any kind? It is frightening enough to have those weapons made in three countries. It will be much more frightening if that manufacture is spread to countries all over the world, and that will happen if something is not done about it because the techniques and the procedures in regard to those matters are becoming known.
It will not be long before there will be a number of governments, some perhaps in the control of people whom we may not trust- I have no particular area of the world in mind when I say that but it may happen in the future-that may all have access to weapons which can destroy the world. While the situation is bad enough now, surely that is infinitely more frightening.
Then there is another matter which is related to the one I have mentioned. I refer to the suspension of tests of nuclear weapons of mass destruction. I think we in Canada should now push the initiative at the United Nations for the abolition of these tests over a period of let us say five years, without any conditions being attached except that of United Nations supervision which, of course, is an important one.
Then there is a third matter which does not involve taking the initiative because Canada has been pressing this at the United Nations for some time, and I believe did so at the last assembly. Is this not a good opportunity in the light of what has happened in the last few months to press forward for the establishment of a permanent United Nations police force? I hope to have something to say about that a little later. Perhaps the atmosphere now is more conducive to progress in that regard than it was a year or two years ago. These, then, are three matters which perhaps might be pushed at the forthcoming assembly of the United Nations.
I come now to the matter to which I shall devote most of my time, as the minister quite rightly did; the situation in the Middle East and more particularly in Lebanon and Jordan. This situation developed quickly, at least in its more critical manifestations of recent days. I know the difficulties the government must have had in trying to make up its mind without very much warning as to the policy that should be pursued. In

appreciation of those difficulties and with some understanding, as we should have, of the responsibilities incumbent upon us, the opposition attempted to be as constructive as possible during these days, not to ask questions merely for the sake of asking questions or which might confuse an already complicated situation and, indeed, to do nothing which would prejudice the maximum degree of unity in this house and throughout the country over an issue which transcends and I hope will continue to transcend partisan considerations. When peace is threatened- and peace was threatened and perhaps still is-we must all be as united as possible in the house and in the country.
That has been the spirit that has animated us on this side during recent days; nevertheless we have our responsibilities as an opposition, and we must discharge them in a way which will result in questions addressed to the government on various aspects of policy. Indeed, we have also a duty to put forward proposals ourselves when we think that is desirable, so I am going to deal with the Middle East question in somewhat more detail than I confess I have ever been called upon to do before either on this side or the other side of the house, and the reason for that is obvious. I am going to try, if I can, to put the problem in perspective, and that will perhaps require a little more discussion of the historical background than would normally be the case.
As I have said, the problem is greater and deeper than its recent manifestations, because they are merely the reflection of a situation which is deep-rooted, difficult and dangerous. That situation, that problem-and it certainly is an international problem-is the emergence of a passionate Arab nationalism which expresses itself at times in bitter and even savage anti-foreignism or anti-imperialism as they more often call it. Perhaps we should not forget that as we have to face the immediate problems that arise from day to day out of this situation.
The situation in its historical perspective has been well put by Professor Smith of the school of Islamic studies at McGill University in his book, "Islam in Modern History", when he says:
For 75 years the Arab has got up in the morning, has lived his life, has pursued his pleasures and his dreams, always under the shadow of guns- guns in alien, unfriendly hands, ready to fire, ready to call in from across the sea more guns, ships, tanks, planes, might. Whether this power was used, as from time to time it shatteringly was, or was merely threatened, as often it cogently could be, or was merely there, always the shadow, the shame, the oppression remained. Whether terror or insult, provocation or opiate, this bitter foreign power has stood, an abiding fact. Any thought
External Affairs
about the Arab world uncoloured by the vivid imagination of this dominating reality is unfruitful, misleading, false.
I know that this feeling, expressed so graphically in this quotation, is fomented, exploited and when possible directed by the forces of the international communist conspiracy and also-and we should not forget this-by Russian imperialism, which is something else. But without communism there would still be trouble in the Middle East and there would still be Russia with her eyes and ambitions on her historic goal in the Mediterranean. That, Mr. Speaker, is the historical background against which we have to consider the crisis facing us today.
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, this would be a good time for me to ask you to call it one o'clock.
At one o'clock the house took recess.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
External Affairs
peace in the Middle East; and also recognition of Arab nationalism based on Arab countries free of Soviet communist threats, free of penetration and subversion, each one governing itself as it desires without interference from or without interfering in neighbouring states.
The second objective is collective security for defence against aggression. That certainly has been an objective of the British government over recent years in this area. The west, led by the British government, has tried to promote that objective of collective security through the Baghdad pact, which, we must not forget, it was hoped would embrace all the Arab states but which has never succeeded in doing so. However, it has split the Arab world into two camps, with the United Kingdom and the United States in one camp or at least with the United States half way in that camp and the other forces in the other camp.
I suggest that the third end that is being sought is security for oil supplies in that area which are vitally important to the whole economy of western Europe and, to a lesser extent, to other parts of the world; the security of navigation through the Suez canal, and the maintenance of legitimate western economic and other interests in the area.
Finally, I suggest as an objective of western policy in that area the right of Israel to a national existence within recognized and agreed boundaries. Of course there have been other objectives and policies, but perhaps these are the main ones.
A couple of weeks ago the violent and sudden overthrow of a friendly regime in Iraq seemed to strike at those policies and to foreshadow not only the end of the Baghdad pact but the revolutionary absorption of Lebanon and Jordan into the United Arab Republic; hence the intervention.
Again the question arises, does the intervention which has taken place strengthen and safeguard the objectives I have mentioned or does it serve to prevent some of the undesirable results which I have also mentioned? I doubt the first, though I admit the pressure which appeared to necessitate intervention at the time. I also admit the possibility of unhappy consequences if the action had not been taken. Presumably there was not very much time. That is one of the tragedies of international affairs these present days; there is never enough time to assess the consequences of action or no action. Presumably on this occasion there was not enough time, certainly not very much time, in which to weigh the disadvantages or advantages of intervention or no intervention because-and this is one of the most worrying features of the whole situation so far as

I am concerned-the outbreak in Iraq seems to have caught the western countries which have the most in the way of intelligence services completely by surprise. Yet we are now told by the authors of this revolution that they had been plotting it for months and years.
It is also now clear, and the minister mentioned this this morning-at least I believe he mentioned it, though if I am misinterpreting what he said he will correct me -that the governments of the United Kingdom and the United States are anxious to liquidate their intervention as quickly as possible and replace their forces by those once again, of the United Nations, for the important purpose of establishing and maintaining the right of Lebanon and Jordan not to be gobbled up, if I can put it that way. That is an understandable policy on the part of London and Washington because it is difficult, at least it is difficult for me, to see anything but difficulty ahead if this intervention has to be maintained.
We ask ourselves this question. Will the United States intervention in Lebanon increase the interference and aid for the rebels from outside, to prevent which was one of the purposes of the intervention? We read in the newspapers today, that the foreign minister of Lebanon is again complaining of assistance to the rebels from outside which he says has increased during the last week.
Another question we can hardly refrain from asking ourselves is what is the continuing objective of the intervention? What happens if King Hussein goes, or if he moves out of Jordan against Iraq? And above all, what effect will this intervention have on Arab nationalism in Lebanon, Jordan and elsewhere? Mr. Hanson Baldwin, writing in the New York Times on July 16, had this to say:
Their mere presence-
That is the mere presence of the United States forces.

in Lebanon will be to Arab nationalists like a red rag to a bull-it will do more than any other event since the Port Said attack to knit together Arab nationalists throughout the Middle East and to inflame them . . . the forces of Arab nationalism, symbolized by President Gamal Abdel Nasser of Egypt, will ultimately be strengthened-not weakened-by the United States action.
The London Economist gave expression to the same thought in a recent edition, and then there is another question that these governments must now be asking themselves. What about the security of the oil pipe lines if popular passions against western intervention should boil over?

However, the most important question of all is what should we do about the situation generally. I was glad to hear the minister say this morning that it is now time to look ahead and perhaps, in attempting to answer the question "What should we do about it?", we are looking ahead. My own effort to answer the question is as follows. I suggest we should recognize that the present situation in the Middle East is very much to the liking of Mr. Khrushchev of the Soviet union, who must be very happy at this western intervention since its major result may well be to stir up anti-western feeling, and who benefits most by this feeling in any part of the world. In that sense perhaps this kind of action is really playing the Russian game. I suggest that Mr. Khrushchev, in spite of all his recent words, may not have any great desire to see the United States and the United Kingdom leave these countries. I believe, however, that he has a very great desire to secure the maximum propaganda out of their being there.
I submit that the second aspect, the second phase of the policy we should adopt, which follows from my answer to the first question, is the withdrawal as soon as possible from these countries by the United Kingdom and the United States, in accordance with the desire they have themselves expressed. However, as we all know it is much easier to land troops in an emergency than it is to withdraw them, and sometimes it is not easy to avoid getting enmeshed even further than was originally intended.
This is where the United Nations comes in, and I am glad to see that that organization is playing its part. The United Nations could help make possible the withdrawal of these forces, which is the desire of the two governments concerned, and perhaps this assistance can now be obtained. It is going to be difficult to negotiate in the security council, as my hon. friend knows, because of the veto used by the Russians with respect to action in that council. Assistance may be obtained, however, through a summit meeting, although a good deal of confusion seems to now be developing over the calling and the composition of such a meeting. It was only a few days ago that we discussed this matter in this house, when Mr. Khrushchev issued his invitation to discuss the Middle East question at a summit meeting.
It seems to me that this was a suggestion which the two powers most concerned, Great Britain and the United States, should have taken up at once, especially in so far as the terms put forward by Mr. Khrushchev regarding the composition were concerned, although they certainly could not have accepted the form of the invitation which was, to
External Affairs
say the least, offensive in character. Surely, however, they could have replied at once that the invitation was acceptable in the sense that the four powers and the secretary general should meet, and meet quickly, and that the meeting should be held under the auspices of the security council.
I personally felt at that time, and I still feel-even more so in the light of developments in the last day or two-that it would have been a good thing for the security council to have been called together at once. They could have set up a committee of the council to consist of the four countries plus India and the secretary general of the United Nations, as mentioned in the invitation of Mr. Khrushchev. Under the chairmanship of the secretary general that committee could have commenced work right away in any place recommended or chosen by the secretary general, with the agreement of the governments concerned. He may well have chosen, although of course I do not know this, Geneva; and while it is not possible for any summit conference to be held without a good deal of publicity, perhaps there might be a little less publicity in Geneva than on the east side of New York.
I do feel, even more strongly than I did a few days ago, that the represention put forward by Mr. Khrushchev for this meeting was a very advantageous one from the point of view of the west, because of its inclusion of the United Kingdom, the United States, France, India-a member of the commonwealth-and the secretary general. I suggest we are now getting away from that sort of clear-cut composition. The press reports would indicate that there is a good deal of manoeuvring going on, not only as to where the meeting should be held but also as to who should attend. Perhaps a solution will be found in a full meeting of the security council, with additional countries invited who have special interests in the problem, as Mr. Khrushchev has suggested, and after a first or second meeting at the summit in the security council in New York perhaps then the countries which were originally mentioned by Mr. Khrushchev might meet under the chairmanship of the secretary general in private sessions, as indeed was the practice during the Suez discussions at New York I think three years ago this summer.
But I cannot myself feel too optimistic about a full meeting of the security council to discuss Middle Eastern matters in this tense and excitable atmosphere with additional governments invited, as Mr. Khrushchev has suggested, to a number not yet determined; a meeting to be held in New York in public in the United Nations. I am

External Affairs
afraid it will be difficult to avoid that kind of public meeting becoming an instrument merely of propaganda.
Mr. Walter Lippmann, who is a pretty wise commentator on these matters, I think, had this to say this morning in his column in the Montreal Gazette:
As things stand at this moment, the notion of a summit meeting in the heart of New York city has the characteristic of one of those nightmares in which one feels compelled to do what one desperately does not want to do.
At this time, a public confrontation between Eisenhower and Khrushchev would be a ghastly spectacle, almost certain to poison the air still further with charges and counter-charges.
I do not think we have to be as pessimistic as that but I do hope, and I feel certain my hope is shared by the government, that if this meeting takes place in the full security council in New York, then advantage will be taken at the earliest opportunity of arranging small and confidential meetings of those most concerned to be held under the auspices of the secretary general himself.
There are two other questions to be considered with regard to policy in the Middle East. After withdrawal, the United Nations I think should move in, if the circumstances require it, and if authority can be secured from the security council, or if not from the United Nations assembly. In referring to moving in I do not want to be too dogmatic as to how it should be done. One way would be by a United Nations emergency force, but another would be the way pointed out by the minister this morning, by strengthening the existing United Nations observer group to a point where it might be able to exercise a pacifying and stabilizing influence in the country in which it is operating.
We on this side heard with much satisfaction the statement of the minister to the effect that the government is prepared to support to the fullest extent action to strengthen that group of United Nations observers. It is encouraging to read in the press that the secretary general, without requiring a further resolution from the security council, has already taken advantage of an earlier resolution to strengthen the observer group. This constitutes another debt we owe to a man of exceptional quality, integrity and ability, the secretary general of the United Nations.
What we have been going through during the last two or three weeks-and I mentioned this earlier in my statement, before lunch- has served to underline and emphasize the necessity of a permanent United Nations emergency force. I do not mean by that 20,000 or 25,000 soldiers in a camp of their

own in some country chosen for that purpose. I mean a force consisting of contingents earmarked and available for service at the request of the United Nations authorities; ready to serve at a moment's notice, forces earmarked by other than permanent members of the security council that would be kept available in their own country for such United Nations service.

speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit a question. He had his experience over the years at the United Nations. Was not that very thing attempted on several occasions, and was it not discontinued because of the fact that it was impossible of attainment? I am not attempting to throw cold water on the suggestion, because I believe in it myself, but I ask the hon. gentleman how that could be achieved in the face of the veto situation.

speechtext:
As the Prime Minister has
pointed out, Mr. Speaker, it was attempted more than once. It was attempted under the provisions of the charter which provide for an international force under the security council. The Prime Minister will remember that at the very beginning of the United Nations an international staff of the permanent members of the security council was set up.

speechtext:
Under article 43 of the
charter, as my hon. friend mentions. I think that this permanent military staff is still in existence, nominally, and I am not sure that it does not even meet once a month or so. It consists of military officers from permanent members of the council. It was frustrated from the beginning by the failure of those members of the council to agree on anything, let alone building up force behind the charter. While it became clear over the years that it could not be done in that way, the Prime Minister will recall that during the Korean crisis the first steps were taken by which the assembly could move in to organize forces when the security council was paralysed by the veto. That was done by an assembly resolution which was called the "Uniting for Peace" resolution. That was the resolution used during the Suez crisis to build up on an ad hoc basis a force which I believe was of assistance and which I believe is still doing good service in that part of the world.
That was done under emergency conditions. The Prime Minister will remember that within 48 hours of the resolution of the United Nations assembly authorizing the creation of this force, the force was formally in existence, and within 72 hours the first members of the force were on the job. But surely we

should not rely on that kind of thing in an emergency. Surely it would be better using the assembly resolution for this purpose, if we cannot do it through the security council, to set up in the countries concerned -and they would have to be the non-permanent members of the security council, omitting the big powers-contingents which would be available for this kind of service if the assembly or the security council requested it; which would be organized for that purpose and which could move into action without delay.
I know that this has been attempted in the last year. I think it was brought up at the last assembly. X am not in a position to criticize anyone because it has not been done, for we have all been trying to do it. But perhaps this second demonstration in an international crisis of the value of this kind of police organism in permanent existence will give us now more chance of success in following the matter up at the next assembly than we had at previous assemblies. That is all I am putting forward at this time.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on that point would the hon. gentleman permit a question. The hon. gentleman used the expression "move into action". Did he mean into military action, or would he care to change that expression?

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker; that was perhaps a careless expression. I meant that it could be moved into police and supervisory action. I know perhaps as well as most hon. members of the house the limitation of this kind of force and indeed the limitation of this kind of action. This force would be of no value at all as a military force in the normal sense. It could not stand up against a big or a middle power. If there were a dispute between the big powers this force would be futile. But as a police force operating as it did in Palestine, and operating as it might in the Middle East now under the authority of the United Nations for police purposes, it might be of great value. All I am suggesting is that if it has any possible value of that kind, that value would be very greatly increased by having the force ready to go into this kind of action when required.
But more important perhaps than the questions I have brought up as to the future policy toward this area is the necessity of following up this immediate crisis by some kind of economic and political solution for problems of the whole area, and I was delighted to hear the minister express that thought this morning. Withdrawal and perhaps replacement by a United Nations police force will not be enough unless we do some-
External Affairs
thing about the political and economic difficulties that brought about the situation in the first place.
I recall very well and with a tragic memory that while in the Suez crisis we may have succeeded in producing a United Nations police force which was of help in that crisis, we failed in our major objective, which was to take advantage of that atmosphere of crisis and do something about the political and economic difficulties between Israel and her neighbours which brought about the crisis in the first place. We did nothing on that front; therefore we did not succeed there even though we may have succeeded in the more limited field of preventing the conflict spreading.
We hope we will not make that mistake this time. I know how easy it will be to make such a mistake after the immediate crisis is solved, but I hope that this time the west will try to work out on a firm and permanent basis its relations with those nationalist forces in that area I have been talking about. I believe that for this purpose the west-and I am thinking of the United States, the United Kingdom and France particularly-must base their relations with those countries on the acceptance of Arab nationalism and of the United Arab Republic; must try to bring about as much co-operation as possible with those forces; try to remove the suspicions which have been engendered over the past and which are not by any means all the fault of the west. They must accept the realities of the present and base their policy on the fact that the nineteenth century is dead and is not likely to return.
I suggest something else, and this is going to be even more difficult politically; that our policy in the Middle East in the future must recognize that the U.S.S.R. has both interest and power in that area. Indeed its power in that area is far greater than that which could be produced in the west to bear upon the problems of that area at any given time. I think we must all be very conscious of the fact that while there are 10,000 United States marines in Lebanon and two or three British paratroop battalions in Jordan, there are 23 Soviet divisions, it is reported, strung along the Iran-Turkish border. Therefore it is idle to pretend the Soviet union need only be tolerating that area. It is also idle to deny the fact that the Soviet union has very real interests in that area which perhaps should be recognized.
The minister said this morning that one of the happy developments of recent years, and a development which might be applied to the Middle East, was the successful operation of the international commissions in Indo-China.

External Affairs
I agree with him, though I also agree with him when he said the time has come to wind up the activities of two of those commissions in the way he mentioned. But he himself also said-and it is an important fact-that in that operation in Indo-China one of the three members of each commission was from a communist state. While it is true that it is a state which is making moves toward communist nationalism, yet at the time it was appointed it was pretty close to the foreign policy and the defence policy of Russia. That was recognized at that time and I was at the Geneva conference when it was accepted that there could be no settlement of the kind desired in Indo-China without a recognition of the participation of the communist world in that settlement. It was done, and the results have not been too bad.
Perhaps if we are going to have a final economic and political settlement in the Middle East we will have to recognize in some appropriate way the interest of the Soviet in that settlement. Perhaps the best way to do that would be to bring any political and economic aid scheme-the minister mentioned it this morning-into the United Nations; a Marshall plan, if you want to call it that, for the Middle East but administered by the United Nations, where perhaps Soviet participation will be less open to exploitation than if it were done in any other way. Indeed they may not wish to participate at all in that kind of plan.
Then finally Mr. Speaker-it will be an important phase of our policy in this area in the future-that we have to continue in the west to give support to Israel's right to a secure national existence. We have got to do more than that with Israel's co-operation and assistance. We have to think of some way of liquidating the Arab refugee problem.
This is a very sketchy outline of the basis of our policy in the Middle East, a policy which I think provides the best hope of strengthening legitimate western influence and strength in that area and at the same time strengthening the chances of peace and security.
The alternative is the pursuit of power politics without sufficient power, or at least sufficient power in the face of the hostility of another and nearer great power which can bring more power to bear on that particular area. That is one alternative, and I certainly hope we will not follow it. But an even worse alternative than that, perhaps, is a policy of drift and uncertainty; of trying to pursue contradictory aims and trying to execute those contradictory aims in a halfhearted and confused way. I suggest the policy which I have ventured to outline in
[Mr. Pearson.l
brief is one of realism and common sense, and one which the west should pursue at this time.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I had hoped to deal with a good many other subjects, but I do not want to take up all the time of the house on this debate. I probably will have another opportunity to discuss these matters. I was going to talk about NATO and its importance in many things, and particularly in this Middle East crisis. I was glad to read in the press this morning that the NATO council is meeting today, as it has been meeting in recent days, to consider developments in the Middle East. It is of the greatest possible importance to strengthen political cooperation through the NATO council not only in the area covered by NATO but in the areas contiguous to the NATO countries which are of vital importance to them.
I also suggest that political co-operation in NATO requires a solution of the difficulties between its members with special interest in the Middle East. Something must be done, for instance to halt the growing bitterness and enmity between the two NATO countries, Turkey and Greece. I have stated a good many times, my view that a military and defence foundation for NATO is not enough, indeed it is necessary now as it was never necessary before to make progress in the field of economic and political co-operation.
Then, Mr. Speaker, there is the most important question of all, and this concerns not merely the Middle East, which is a reflection of the importance of this general question. What can we do at this time to ease tensions and remove or diminish some of the dangers of war? The minister touched upon the matter this morning, but it really deserves far more time than we can give to it in a debate of this kind. But I suggest, however, as I have suggested many times, that we should not allow the crises of the moment to prevent us continuing to seek solutions of our problems with the Soviet union through diplomatic and political channels. We should not only keep our defence strong-we have to do that, though it is a little difficult these days to know what kind of defence should be kept-but we have to keep our diplomacy enlightened and imaginative and vigorous.
The fact that we all feel-and I think we have felt it more in the last two weeks than for quite a long time-the fear of what we call in diplomacy brinkmanship should not obscure the fact that even without that kind of diplomacy, even without those tactics which at times may worry us, even without brinkmanship, we remain on the brink of

extinction. This is true because of the developments in nuclear warfare, because of the piling up of weapons of mass destruction which if they are ever used can make life on this planet impossible. We do not need brinkmanship to emphasize that we are indeed on the brink of that kind of extinction if we allow diplomacy to degenerate into conflict or the world to slide into general war, which is perhaps the only way we will get in. We have existed in this way now for more than 10 years.
We have existed in a world which is bedevilled by a combination, as I have put it before, of hate and hydrogen, of fear and ferocity. That combination still overhangs our life. Our policy surely in this country, and in all free countries, must be to bring about the replacement of that kind of thing by some form of security, on the basis at least of mutual toleration, if we cannot do any better than that, between those who must coexist but cannot co-operate, plus-and this is equally important-closer and closer co-operation between those states which can and must work together for their very survival. That, I suggest to the house, is the only policy that makes sense today. We are all proud as Canadians to know that Canada has played, and I am sure is playing and will continue to play, a good and proud part in the pursuit of that policy. Perhaps I know as well as most Canadians how terribly difficult this part is, how exhausting at times it is and, as I said at the beginning of my statement and as the minister must have found, -how frustrating it often is. At times it seems so much easier to fall back into our foxholes, into our national trenches, to dig ourselves in there and wait for what may happen. Movement is hard and at times we wonder where we are going; or if we are going anywhere. We reach a green pasture and we find that there is a greener pasture beyond. We scale a peak and we find a higher one barring the way. As a poet puts it, "We are forever climbing the ever-mounting slope". But I know all members of the house will agree with me when I say that is no reason for giving up but is a reason for continuing to climb.
I know the house will also agree with me when I say that in this search for peace in a better world all members of the house, irrespective of the party to which they may belong, as indeed all Canadians, will be happy and proud to work together.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is without doubt an important day in the present session. An opportunity is accorded for the free expression of the views of members with respect to international
External Affairs
affairs and the crises that face our country and all countries of the world. It is to me, of course, a very unexpected and unusual experience to have to follow the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Smith) of the present government and the secretary of state for external affairs of the previous government. I am the first one to admit, sir, that I do not know the intricacies and strategies of inner diplomacy as they must be known by the two previous speakers because of the present position of the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the past experience of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson).
Therefore it follows that I do not intend to go into the intricate details of strategy or policy, but I do welcome this opportunity to put forward a few general thoughts from the viewpoint of a layman. I feel quite certain that in taking part in the first discussion of external affairs this session we can all start from the same fundamental belief, namely that nobody wants to see another world war. On that premise we have to consider developments as they occur.
In the present century the major countries of the world have seen two world wars in which countless billions of dollars in productive effort have been expended in the holocaust of war. In addition millions of men, women and children have either died or been mutilated. No one wants to see that happen again, and in saying that we have particular reference to the scientific and technological developments of recent years from which it is known by all that a third world war could possibly mean the annihilation of civilization as we understand it at the present time.
This leads me to make the observation that a world war can start from a spark in international relations in the same way as a catastrophic fire. In my own province of British Columbia right now there are almost one million acres on fire, a fire that could have started from a bolt of lightning, a carelessly thrown match or a cigarette that was not put out. So it is in war. Officially at least the first world war started because an archduke was assassinated. Officially at least the second world war started because of the aggression of one country, because of the insanity of one man.
That leads us, therefore, to the realization that as nobody wants to see another world war, very close attention must be paid to international affairs and relationships to see that with modern weapons, technology and science no spark occurs to lead the world into a conflagration which could mean the end of civilization. If that is accepted, and I think logically it may well be, we have to approach our external affairs and relationships not only on the basis of day to day

External Affairs
developments but on the basis of what has given rise to these developments.
There may be those who will not agree with me, which is understandable, but I quite honestly feel that if we are truly going to play our part and take every possible action to preserve peace we must understand what gives rise to certain actions by certain countries. In the past few years our major troubles have developed in the Middle East.
I have not yet seen any factual denial that even in connection with the Suez crisis it was not a matter of country against country but was a matter of the protection of oil interests. In these past few weeks we have again seen a Middle East crisis. I believe it would mean a great deal if we could be told whether or not the armed intervention was on an anti-communist basis or for the protection of certain oil interests. Personally, I am not going to state any conclusion, but I do consider this something upon which there has not been any government consideration or public answer.
I am convinced that nobody wants war. We can make the definite statement that Canada does not want war, nor do I believe that any of the western democracies want war. In view of that fact, I am led to ask if Canada could not play a greater part in advising on the present international crisis? We recognize that Canada is not a major power in the world but it is, if I can use the terms, a middle power. It is my definite belief that because Canada at no time has had imperialistic or colonial ambitions, and because of its economic strength Canada could play a most significant role in these very critical days.
When this present Middle East crisis developed I will say I was most disappointed in the first pronouncements that were made by this government. I interpreted them, and I think the majority of the press across Canada interpreted the statements as unqualified support of United States policy. I hasten to add that it was with appreciation and gratitude that, in very short order, we did see leadership and direction coming from the government, and not a supine following of the United States. There was a recognition of the seriousness of the situation, and very definite representations to deal with the crisis. Personally, I feel proud of the direction that was given after the first pronouncement, and I hope that direction may have had some effect upon the developments of recent days and the changed policies. The result has been that Canada has given some leadership on the calling of a summit meeting.
I listened very intently to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Smith) in

what he had to say today, but I have one regret. He failed to give to this house any indication of how strong a position Canada is going to take in view of the recent pronouncements made by, or on behalf of, the President of the United States. We in this corner of the house believed even up until yesterday that some country of the western world had to speak very clearly and bluntly to the United States about its foreign policy with regard to the present Middle East situation. Personally, I cannot understand why, if we truly believe that our economy is the best in the world, that our democracy is the best, we are afraid-when I say "we" I mean as western democratic powers-to meet with anybody else in this world face to face. Quite honestly, Mr. Speaker, I think that the prestige, the influence of the free powers has slipped within the past few days if what appears in the press is correct. According to press reports the government of the United States is disturbed that Khrushchev has accepted the invitation to a summit meeting in New York. There are statements, and perhaps we will have more information about them, that they fear Khrushchev would use such a meeting for propaganda purposes.
I am not going to go into any more detail about that, Mr. Speaker, except to say that if we believe in our way of life, if we believe in our democratic system, then we need have no fear of meeting the leader of any country, any time, anywhere, especially if it may be the basis upon which some agreement may be reached to settle the present mid-eastem crisis and prevent a conflict that could possibly lead to a third world war.
This is a general discussion on external affairs, so may I add this. I know it is of importance to the Prime Minister (Mr. Dief-enbaker) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs, but I direct my remarks in particular to the Prime Minister: I am not in any way derogatory of efforts made by his government or the previous government towards the cessation of nuclear tests or on behalf of world disarmament. But I should like, on behalf of the group in this corner of the house, to ask if still greater emphasis could not De put upon the efforts of the Prime Minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs as between their counterparts in other governments, in the United Nations security council, the United Nations general assembly and special committees, to drive home the absolute essentiality of the cessation of nuclear tests for war purposes and disarmament if we are to avoid another world war.
We must be honest at all times. Today we have a world armament race; you can call it a defence against another country but the

other country is saying the same thing. So whilst we work on defence, we also work on offence. I think the history of the world proves that if you build weapons of offence and defence, eventually you use them. As I said before, I am saying nothing derogatory on what the Prime Minister has worked for in the past. I am just asking that in following up-and I am certain the direction has come from the Prime Minister in the present Middle East crisis-that additional emphasis be placed along the lines which I have just suggested.
We in this group completely agree-and we emphasize this point-that you cannot sit on the fence or play both ends against the middle. The western powers agree on collective security or they do not. We believe in collective security. If we are going to have collective security in the democratic countries it must not be broken down or betrayed. That is why in this house and in our convention which is still going on in Montreal we have expressed our regrets and our condemnation of the countries-yes, of the United States to the south of us and the United Kingdom in which I was born-taking independent action in the landing of troops of their own volition without going through the collective security agency which we are trying to build up, which we support and in which we are all partners. If the United Nations general assembly means anything or if the United Nations security council means anything and if it is going to have a proper respect in this world, it must be because those who are partners in it follow through on collective action. Anything else is not only a betrayal of the meaning of collective security but is making a gift of a propaganda weapon and putting it in the hands of those who we are told are our enemies and who will use it to best advantage.
Mr. Speaker, I said just a few words this afternoon about the exigencies of absence. Very often the Prime Minister, because of the responsibilities of his office, is obliged to be away. We all understand that. Various cabinet ministers, because of their responsibilities and the exigencies of their offices, also are obliged to be away. Private members also very often are obliged to be away. We in our group find ourselves in a similar position because our biennial convention is being held this week and, as I think you will all understand, it is rather important that some M.P.'s be at that convention to discuss national and international politics. Unfortunately, I was not able to be there. However, learning that certain members were not able to return in time for this discussion this afternoon, I was on the telephone for about 30 minutes speaking to a colleague in Montreal in between the
External Affairs
lunch hour and now. We are a democratic party and hold a democratic convention representative of our movement across the length and breadth of Canada. I said, "I am going to have to speak this afternoon. What is the viewpoint of the national convention representative of our movement all across Canada with regard to the present situation?"

speechtext: Are you asking for the party line?

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: No. I asked for the democratic decision of our representatives from all across Canada.
